lessons.title: What is a structure chart?
lessons.summary: Show and read algorithms as a series of clear steps.

steps.title: An algorithm is an exact set of instructions

blocks.text: An **algorithm** describes step by step how to solve a task. Every step must be so clear that someone can carry it out without asking, a person just as well as a computer.
You know algorithms from everyday life: a recipe, directions to a place or the instructions for building a wardrobe.

blocks.caption: Making tea as a structure chart: every box is one step.

steps.title: How to read a structure chart

blocks.text: You read a structure chart **from top to bottom**. Every box is one step. Only when a step is finished does the next one start.
This way of drawing was invented by **Isaac Nassi and Ben Shneiderman** (1973). That is why it is also called a Nassi-Shneiderman diagram. In Germany it is standardised as DIN 66261.

blocks.caption: Left: Isaac “Ike” Nassi (photo: [Ed Schipul](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Me_with_Ike_Nassi!!!!!_%286893328729%29.jpg), [CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/), cropped), right: Ben Shneiderman (photo: [Robert Kosara](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ben_Shneiderman_at_UNCC_%283x4_cropped%29.jpg), CC0).

blocks.text: A structure chart always has exactly one start (at the top) and one end (at the bottom). There are no arrows and no jumps all over the place.

Baaah, listen up! In 1972 Nassi and Shneiderman were still PhD students at Stony Brook University near New York. Shneiderman was about 25 and Nassi about 23. So basically two students who wrote computer science history on the side.
Every algorithm can be built from just **three basic building blocks**: **sequence**, **branch** and **loop**. In this step and the next two you get to know them one by one.
The **sequence** is the simplest building block: several statements run **one after another**, each exactly once.
This is what it looks like:

items: Every statement is a **simple rectangle**.
The rectangles sit **on top of each other** without a gap.
They run from top to bottom, one statement after the other.

blocks.caption: Four statements as a sequence. First you get up, then you brush your teeth, and so on.

blocks.text: The tea example above is a sequence, too.
15 minutes! That is how long Shneiderman needed for the first sketch with sequence, branch and loop. I need longer than that to choose between hay and clover.
Often the next step depends on a **condition**. A condition is a question you can only answer with **yes or no**, for example *Is it raining?* In VisuStruct yes is **true** and no is **false**.
For decisions like this there is the **branch**. This is what it looks like:

items: At the top, the condition sits in a **triangle**.
Below it, the box splits into **two columns**: on the left the path for **true**, on the right the path for **false**.
**Only one** of the two paths ever runs. After that, both paths continue together below the branch.

blocks.caption: If it is raining, the left path runs, otherwise the right one. After that, both cases continue with “Leave”.

blocks.text: If nothing should happen in one case, that path stays empty. The sign **ø** shows this.
Spelling alert! It is Shneiderman, with no c. Anyone who writes “Schneiderman” gets a gentle nudge from my horns. He himself points out that people keep sneaking a c into his name.
If something should happen **several times**, you do not write it down several times. Instead you use a **loop**, also called repetition.
This is what it looks like:

items: At the top is the condition, for example *Plate not empty*.
The steps that are repeated are **indented** below it. On the left, the box forms a **bracket** around them.
Before every pass the condition is checked. As long as it is **true**, the steps inside the bracket run once more. If it is **false**, the program continues below the loop.

blocks.caption: As long as the plate is not empty, you take a bite. After that, the plate is cleared.

blocks.text: There are more kinds of loops. You will meet them in later lessons.
The building blocks become really useful when you combine them. This diagram contains all three: a sequence from top to bottom, a branch and a loop.

blocks.caption: You recognise the branch by its triangle and the loop by the bracket on the left. Everything together sits in a sequence.

blocks.text: The boxes can also be **nested** inside each other: a loop or a path can contain sequences, branches and loops again.

Comfort for anyone who has messed up a test: the famous journal *Communications of the ACM* rejected the structure chart article. According to Nassi, the reviewer even said they should collect every copy and burn it. Ouch! It then appeared in 1973 in a smaller journal and today it is quoted thousands of times. Ha! [More fun facts](https://visustruct.org/en/angeberwissen.html)

steps.title: Other ways to draw it: flowchart and pseudocode

blocks.text: A structure chart is not the only way to write down an algorithm. You will meet two more in class. Here you see the same tea example as above in all three forms.
Flowchart

A **flowchart** is made of symbols joined by **arrows**. It is standardised as DIN 66001 (ISO 5807). A diamond is a decision with the exits yes and no. You recognise a loop by an arrow that leads **back up**.

blocks.caption: The tea example as a flowchart. The arrow from “Wait 1 minute” back up forms the loop.

blocks.text: Pseudocode
**Pseudocode** is text that looks like a program but is written in plain language. Fixed words such as IF and WHILE show the building blocks, and the **indentation** shows what belongs to them.

Put a cup on the table
IF sugar wanted THEN
    Add sugar
END IF
WHILE tea still too hot
    Wait 1 minute
END WHILE
Drink the tea
Compared

items: **Structure chart:** boxes inside boxes, the loop is a bracket on the left. You see the structure at a glance, and wild jumps are impossible.
**Flowchart:** symbols with arrows, the loop is an arrow back up. Very easy to picture, but big charts quickly get confusing.
**Pseudocode:** text with indentation, the loop sits between WHILE and END WHILE. Quick to write and already close to program code.

blocks.text: All three describe the same algorithm. Once you can read one form, you learn the others quickly.

Nassi and Shneiderman were out to get the arrows! Their 1973 article was called “Flowchart Techniques for Structured Programming”. With arrows you can jump all over the place until the chart looks like a plate of spaghetti. In a structure chart that is simply impossible. Baah, that is how I like it: tidy, like my stable.
When you program, two things happen at once: you have to think about the steps and pay attention to how the programming language is written. A structure chart lets you keep the two apart.

items: First you think about the **logic**: which steps, which conditions, which repetitions?
Then you translate the finished structure into **Java, Python or JavaScript**. VisuStruct can even generate the code for you.

blocks.text: With the **simulation** you can also run your structure chart step by step and check whether it really does what it should.

Programs that jump all over the place are called **spaghetti code**: if you try to follow one thread, you get tangled up like in a plate of spaghetti. In the old days the culprit was the GOTO command, meaning “jump to line …”. So in 1968 the computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra wrote a famous letter: “Go To Statement Considered Harmful”. Since then, programs are built only from sequence, branch and loop. In Java, `goto` is still a reserved word today, but you are not allowed to use it. Baah, I would rather eat spaghetti than program it.

items.text: I can explain what an algorithm is.
I know that a structure chart is read from top to bottom.
I know the three basic building blocks: sequence, branch and loop.
I can recognise every building block in a structure chart by its shape.
I can also read a simple algorithm as a flowchart and as pseudocode.

options.text: By a bracket on the left side
By an arrow that leads back up

lessons.title: The editor
lessons.summary: Insert elements, type text, move and delete.

blocks.text: The editor has several areas. Move the mouse over a blue word or tap it, and that area lights up in the editor.

items: **At the very top, the toolbar:** New, Open and Save. On the far right, the gear for Settings: text size and language.

**Below it, the tools** above the elements and the structure chart: Undo, Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, Export, Code and Simulation. The buttons only show icons. Hold the mouse over one and its name appears.
**On the left, the Elements:** Here are all the building blocks you can drag into the structure chart. Some people also call this area the palette.
**In the middle, the structure chart:** A new diagram contains only an empty placeholder, marked with **ø**.
**At the bottom, the Object Inspector:** Here you edit the text of the selected element.

blocks.text: You can collapse this learning area at any time with the sidebar icon at the top of this area. Then only the slim “🎓 Learn” strip stays on the left; click it to open the area again. It stays open next to the editor so you can try out right away what you read. In the same way there is the 📁 Files column on the left for your saved programs (lesson 3) and the Programming area on the right for Java (lesson 20).
Drag an element from the **Elements** area onto the structure chart. While you drag, a blue line shows where it will land:

items: **Onto the placeholder ø:** The element replaces the placeholder.
**Onto the top half of a box:** The element goes in front of it.
**Onto the bottom half of a box:** The element goes after it.

blocks.caption: Where you drop it decides where the new element lands.

blocks.text: You can also select an element in the Elements area with the keyboard and press **Enter**. Then it is inserted after the selected box.

Grabbing boxes and dragging them around, just like you are doing now, has a fancy name: **direct manipulation**. Ben Shneiderman coined the term in 1982. Yes, the structure chart guy. That man worked harder than I do when I graze. [More about him](https://visustruct.org/en/angeberwissen.html)
Click a box. It gets a blue outline, and its text appears in the Object Inspector below the diagram. Whatever you type there shows up in the diagram straight away.
The box from the Elements area is called a **Statement**. At the top of the Object Inspector you choose what sort of statement it should be:

items: **Statement:** calculate or set something, e.g. `int number = 5`. You will learn how in lesson 4.
**Input:** ask for a value while the chart runs. That comes in lesson 6.
**Output:** show something. In the diagram it then has `output:` in front, e.g. `output: "Hello"`.

blocks.text: To start with, you only need Output. Texts that should be shown exactly as they are go in **quotation marks**.

blocks.caption: Two outputs one after the other. Open the diagram in the editor and start the simulation to see the output.

items: **Move:** Drag an existing box to a new place with the mouse.
**Copy and paste:** Select a box, then press Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V (on a Mac ⌘C and ⌘V). The copy goes after the selected box.
**Delete:** Select a box and press Del.
**Undo:** Ctrl+Z undoes the last step, Ctrl+Shift+Z brings it back.

exercise.title: Hello World

task.text: Build a structure chart that outputs **Hello World**. Drag a Statement onto the placeholder, set it to **Output** in the Object Inspector and type `"Hello World"`.

hints: You only need one single box. The text that should appear goes into the text field in the Object Inspector.
Watch out for the quotation marks. Without them, VisuStruct looks for a variable called Hello.

blocks.text: Click **Check** when you are done. VisuStruct runs your structure chart and compares the output.

exercise.title: Two lines

task.text: First output **Hello** and then **I am learning structure charts**, each on its own line.

hints: Two lines means two outputs. The boxes sit on top of each other and run from top to bottom.
Every output is a box of its own. Drag the second Statement onto the bottom half of the first one.

items.text: I can insert an element from the Elements area and replace a placeholder.
I can change the text of a box and switch between Statement, Input and Output.
I can move, copy and delete boxes and undo steps.

lessons.title: Save, open, export
lessons.summary: Keep your files safe, use the workspace with class folders, open several diagrams and share them as an image or PDF.

blocks.text: Structure charts are saved as **.visustruct** files. All versions of VisuStruct use the same format: in the browser, on Mac, iPad and iPhone, and the Java app on the computer. So you can start in the browser at school and carry on in the app at home.

When Nassi was a student, there were no files to save. There were punched cards. Nassi says a Saturday night date looked like this: his future wife sat with him in the computer centre and punched his cards. Romance, computer science style!

items: **Save** (Ctrl+S): The diagram is saved as a file. If the **Files** column is set up (see below), it goes there. Otherwise the browser asks where to put it or puts the file in your downloads folder.
**Open** (Ctrl+O): Load a saved file again. You can also simply drag a file into the browser window.

blocks.text: The browser remembers your exercises automatically. But that only works in this browser on this device. So always save important work as a file as well.
To the left of the learning area you find the 📁 Files column. There you keep all your programs in one place, your **workspace**.

items: Open the column and set up the workspace. In Chrome and Edge you choose a folder on your computer for it, for example in your documents. On the iPad and in other browsers, VisuStruct saves in the browser.
Use the folder icon with **+** to create a folder for your class, for example `11FI1`. Clicking a class folder makes it the current **class**.
Save as usual. In your class, VisuStruct automatically creates a folder with today's date, for example `2026-10-23`, and saves the program in it. The file name comes from the title.

blocks.text: Clicking a program in the column opens it again. That way you quickly find every lesson later.

Your **learning progress** goes into the workspace too: the file `lernstand.json` lists the lessons and exercises you have finished. If you open the workspace in another browser, your progress is back.
Browser storage only stays in this browser on this device. A real folder on your computer is safer, because you can also back it up and pass it on.
Above the structure chart you see the tabs. With **+** or New you open another, empty diagram. A dot • in front of the name shows that there are unsaved changes.
You type the title of a diagram into the field above the structure chart. It also appears when you export and is suggested as the file name.

steps.title: Share as an image or PDF

blocks.text: With Export in the tools (icon with an arrow pointing up) you can share your structure chart:

items: **Image (PNG):** to put into a worksheet or a presentation
**Vector graphic (SVG):** stays sharp at any size
**PDF (A4):** one page to hand in or print
**Print** (Ctrl+P): straight to the printer

blocks.text: Under the gear at the top right, Text size sets the font size. Larger text also shows when you export an image.

steps.title: Game: How do you pass it on?

blocks.text: Open one of your exercises from lesson 2 and try the following:

items.text: I have given the diagram a title.
I have saved the diagram as a .visustruct file and opened it again.
I have exported the diagram as an image (PNG) or PDF.
I have opened a second diagram in a new tab.
I have created a class folder in the Files column and saved into it.

Because the browser only keeps the data on this device and it can get lost
Because you cannot export without saving

lessons.title: Variables and data types
lessons.summary: Store values, get to know the data types int, double, String and boolean, and calculate.

blocks.text: A **variable** is like a labelled box. It has a **name**, a **data type** and a **value**.
int age = 14
Here the variable is called `age`, its data type is `int` (whole number), and its value is 14. You can use the value again later through its name.

blocks.caption: The variable as a box: the name on the label, the data type as a sticker, the value inside.

blocks.text: Variable names start with a letter and contain no spaces. Good names say what is inside: `price` is better than `p`.
The data type says what kind of value may be stored in the variable.

items: **int:** whole numbers, e.g. `int count = 3` or `int temperature = -5`
**double:** decimal numbers, e.g. `double price = 2.5`. You write a **point**, never a comma.
**String:** text, e.g. `String name = "Mia"`. Text goes in quotation marks.
**boolean:** truth values, only `true` or `false`

blocks.caption: Three variables with different data types. Open the diagram and start the simulation.

blocks.text: You mostly meet truth values in **conditions**: `age >= 18` is either `true` or `false`. That is what lesson 8 is about. You can also store the result of a condition in a variable:

int age = 15
boolean adult = age >= 18
After that, `adult` holds the value `false`.
The sign `=` is called an **assignment**. It does not mean “equals” as in maths. It means: work out the right-hand side and store the result in the variable on the left.

int points = 10
points = points + 5

In maths the second line would be wrong, because no number equals itself plus 5. In programming you read it like this: take the old value 10, add 5 and store 15 in `points`. You only write the data type the first time, when the variable is created.

blocks.caption: First the right-hand side is calculated, then the result lands in the variable on the left.

blocks.text: You can calculate with numbers:

items: `+` plus, `-` minus, `*` times, `/` divided by
`%` remainder of a division, e.g. `17 % 5` is 2

blocks.text: **Multiplication and division come before addition and subtraction**, and brackets are worked out first: `2 * (3 + 4)` is 14.

exercise.title: Work out a rectangle

task.text: A rectangle is 7 long and 4 wide. Create the variables `length` and `width`. Calculate the area and the perimeter in variables of their own and output both, like this: `Area: 28` and on the next line `Perimeter: 22`.

hints: First think about which variables you need: two for the measurements and two for the results. They are all whole numbers.
The area is length times width, the perimeter is 2 times (length plus width). For the output you write e.g. `output: "Area: " + area`. The `+` joins the text and the value of the variable together.

blocks.text: If you divide two whole numbers and store the result in an `int` variable, everything after the decimal point is dropped. It is **not rounded**.

int x = 7 / 2      gives 3
int r = 7 % 2      gives 1 (the remainder)
double d = 7.0 / 2 gives 3.5
With `/` and `%` together you can convert things nicely, for example minutes into hours and minutes:

blocks.caption: 135 minutes are 2 hours (135 / 60) with 15 minutes left over (135 % 60).

exercise.title: Convert seconds

task.text: 200 seconds should be output as minutes and seconds. The first and the last statement are already there. Insert statements between them that calculate `minutes` and `remainder`.

hints: How many whole minutes fit into 200 seconds, and how many seconds are left over? Work it out in your head first.
A minute has 60 seconds. Use `/` for the whole minutes and `%` for the remainder. Both variables have the type `int`.

exercise.title: Shopping

task.text: You buy 3 exercise books at 2.5 euros each. Create `count` as an `int` and `price` as a `double`, calculate the total price in a variable `total` and output `Total: 7.5 euros`.

hints: The count times the price gives the total price. For each variable, think about whether it is a whole number or a decimal number.
The total price is a decimal number, so `total` needs the type `double`.

blocks.text: A structure chart is a plan. For a computer to carry it out, you write it down in a programming language, for example in **Java**. The variables from above look like this in Java:

items: You create a variable in Java just like in the box: first the data type, then the name, then the value.
Every statement ends with a **semicolon** `;`.
`String` starts with a capital letter, `int`, `double` and `boolean` are lower case. Java tells upper and lower case apart.
An output is called `System.out.println(…)` in Java.

blocks.text: You type Java in the Programming area to the right of the structure chart. While you type, VisuStruct builds the structure chart along with it. So you see straight away which box belongs to which line.

exercise.title: Profile in Java

task.text: Write a profile of Ludwig the billy goat. Create three variables: the name **Ludwig**, the age **7** and the height **1.2**. Then output these two lines: **Ludwig is 7 years old.** and **Height: 1.2 m** “Open in editor” also opens the Programming area on the right. Type your code there; the structure chart builds itself. Then click Check.

hints: You need a `String`, an `int` and a `double`. Every line ends with a semicolon.
`String name = "Ludwig";`, `int age = 7;` and `double height = 1.2;`. You join the output with `+`: `System.out.println(name + " is " + age + " years old.");`

items.text: I can create a variable with a data type, a name and a value.
I know the data types int, double, String and boolean.
I know that = is an assignment and not a comparison.
I can calculate with + - * / % and know whole-number division.
I can create and output variables in Java.

questions.question: Which data type fits the value 3.75?
questions.explanation: Decimal numbers have the type double. In VisuStruct you write them with a point.

questions.question: What value does x have after `int x = 17 / 5`?
questions.explanation: With whole numbers, everything after the decimal point is dropped. It is not rounded.

questions.question: What does `17 % 5` give?
questions.explanation: 17 divided by 5 is 3, remainder 2. The operator % gives the remainder.

questions.question: At the start, `int points = 10`. What is in points after `points = points * 2`?
questions.explanation: The right-hand side is calculated with the old value 10, and the result 20 is stored in points.

questions.question: Which line correctly creates a decimal number in Java?
questions.explanation: Decimal numbers use a point, and the line ends with a semicolon.

lessons.title: Sequence
lessons.summary: Run steps one after another, watch the order and swap values.

blocks.text: A **sequence** is a series of steps that run exactly once and in exactly this order. In the structure chart the boxes simply sit on top of each other.
Each box only starts when the box above it is finished. Nothing is skipped and nothing is repeated.
The sequence is the simplest of the three basic building blocks. Almost every structure chart is mostly made of sequences.
When you make tea, you notice straight away if the order is wrong. With calculations it is just the same, only it is harder to spot.

blocks.caption: First double, then add 1: the result is 7. If you swap the two middle boxes, you get 8.

blocks.text: The statement `number = number * 2` means: take the value of `number`, multiply it by 2 and store the result in `number` again. So what is in `number` depends on what happened before.
Structure charts are not just school stuff. According to Shneiderman, companies like IBM and Siemens planned their programs with them too. So you are learning pro stuff here. Baaa-mazing!

exercise.title: Put in order

task.text: The start diagram has the right boxes, but in the wrong order. Move them so that **20** is output at the end.

hints: Read each box and ask yourself: which variable does it need, and where does that variable get its value?
A variable has to be created before you calculate with it. The output comes right at the end. Check in your head: (2 + 3) · 4 = 20.

blocks.text: Imagine two glasses: one with juice, one with water. If you want to swap what is in them, you need a third, empty glass.
It is exactly the same with variables. If you simply write `a = b` and then `b = a`, the old value of `a` is already lost. In the end both variables have the same value.
The solution is a **temporary variable** that keeps the old value for a short time:

blocks.caption: Three steps with an empty glass: first the juice into temp, then the water to the left, then the juice from temp to the right.
First a is kept in temp. Then a gets the value of b, and b gets the kept value from temp.

exercise.title: Swap glasses

task.text: The left glass holds juice, the right one water. Swap the contents of the variables `left` and `right` before they are output. Do not change the first two boxes. Insert new statements between them instead.

hints: How do you swap two full glasses in real life? You need a third, empty glass.
Create a temporary variable with `String temp = left`. After that you need two more assignments.

blocks.text: As in lesson 4, you can also write a sequence directly in Java. The swap from above looks like this:

items: Every box becomes one line. The lines run from top to bottom, just like the boxes.
Every statement ends with a **semicolon** `;`.
An output is called `System.out.println(…)` in Java. Mind the capital S in `System`: Java tells upper and lower case apart.

blocks.text: You type Java in the Programming area to the right of the structure chart. While you type, VisuStruct builds the structure chart along with it. So you see straight away which box belongs to which line.

exercise.title: Cinema tickets in Java

task.text: A cinema ticket costs 9 euros. Write a Java program that calculates the price of 3 tickets and outputs **Total: 27**. “Open in editor” also opens the Programming area on the right. Type your code there; the structure chart builds itself. Then click Check.

hints: You need three variables: the price, the number of tickets and the result. Every line ends with a semicolon.
`int price = 9;` and `int count = 3;` create the variables. `int total = price * count;` calculates, and `System.out.println("Total: " + total);` outputs the result.

items.text: I know that a sequence runs from top to bottom.
I can explain why the order of the steps matters.
I can swap two values with a temporary variable.
I can write a sequence in Java.

questions.question: How often does each box of a sequence run?

options.text: Not at all if it is empty

questions.explanation: In a sequence nothing is repeated and nothing is skipped. Loops are there for repetition.

questions.question: At the start a = 5 and b = 9. Then `a = b` runs and after that `b = a`. What is in the variables at the end?
questions.explanation: After `a = b` the old value 5 is lost. `b = a` then only copies the 9 back.

questions.question: Why do you need a temporary variable when swapping?

options.text: So that a value is not overwritten before it is needed
So that the structure chart gets longer
Because otherwise you cannot output variables

questions.question: What does the sequence `int x = 4`, `x = x + 1`, `x = x * 3`, `output: x` output?
questions.explanation: First x becomes 5, then 15.

questions.question: What does every statement end with in Java?
questions.explanation: If the semicolon is missing, VisuStruct shows a hint below the code.

lessons.title: Input and output
lessons.summary: Ask for values, show results and use the IPO model.

blocks.text: Many programs work in three parts:

items: **Input:** The program asks for values, e.g. two numbers.
**Process:** It calculates with the values.
**Output:** It shows the result.

blocks.text: The first letters give **IPO**. So far the values were fixed in the structure chart. With an input, a different value can be used every time the chart runs.

blocks.caption: Input at the top, process in the middle, output at the bottom. Start the simulation and try different numbers.

blocks.text: An input asks for a value while the chart runs and stores it in a variable. You write the **data type**, the **name** and a **question** in quotation marks:

input: int age "How old are you?"
input: double price "Price in euros?"
input: String name "What is your name?"
In the editor you choose the kind **Input** at the top of a Statement. The word `input:` is then already in front, and you only type `int age "How old are you?"`.
The data type decides what may be typed in. With `int`, the simulation reports an error if someone types 2.5 or Hello.
An output shows text and values. Text goes in quotation marks, variables do not. With `+` you **join** the parts together:

output: "Hello " + name + "!"
output: "You are " + age + " years old."
Watch out for the spaces inside the quotation marks. Without them everything sticks together, and you see `HelloMia!` instead of `Hello Mia!`.

exercise.title: Greeting

task.text: Ask for a name and greet the person. When Ada is typed in, **Hello Ada!** should be output.

hints: First comes an input for the name, then an output that uses the name.
The name is text, so the input needs the type `String`. In the output you join `"Hello "`, the variable and `"!"` with `+`.

blocks.text: In an output, `+` **always** joins the parts together, even with numbers. If `a` is 3 and `b` is 4, then
output: a + b
does not show 7 but **34**. So calculate in a variable first and then output the variable:

int sum = a + b
output: "Sum: " + sum
That also fits the IPO model: you calculate in the process part, not in the output.

steps.title: From the task to the structure chart

blocks.text: Before you drag the first box, read the task carefully and take it apart. This is called **problem analysis**. Three questions help you:

items: **What is given?** These values become the **input**. Also think about the data type.
**What are you looking for?** That becomes the **output**.
**How do you get from what is given to what you are looking for?** That is the **process**, often a formula.

blocks.text: An example: *A cinema ticket costs 9 euros. The program asks how many tickets someone buys and shows the total price.*

items: Given: the number of tickets → `input: int count "How many tickets?"`
Looking for: the total price → `output: "Total price: " + total`
Way: count times 9 → `int total = count * 9`

blocks.text: Now you only have to put the three parts on top of each other in the order I, P, O.
Look out for signal words in the task: *asks*, *reads in* or *enters* point to an input. *Shows*, *outputs* or *reports* point to an output.

exercise.title: Sum and product

task.text: Ask for two whole numbers. Then output their sum and their product, each on its own line. With 3 and 4 it looks like this: `Sum: 7` and `Product: 12`.

hints: Plan the order: first read in both numbers, then calculate, then output.
You need two inputs, two statements for calculating and two outputs. Calculate the sum in a variable of its own, otherwise `+` joins the numbers together.

exercise.title: Mean

task.text: Ask for two numbers, which may also be decimal numbers. Output their mean, so for 2 and 3 that is `Mean: 2.5`.

hints: You get the mean of two numbers by adding them and halving the result.
For decimal numbers you use the type `double`. The mean is the sum divided by 2. Remember the brackets: `(x + y) / 2`.

blocks.text: This is the IPO example from the start in Java:

items: For input, Java needs a **Scanner**. You write the first two lines once at the very top, then you can read as often as you like.
`scanner.nextInt()` reads a whole number, `scanner.nextDouble()` a decimal number and `scanner.next()` a word.
The question to the user is a normal output right before it. VisuStruct turns both lines together into one input box.

exercise.title: Age in days

task.text: Write a Java program that asks for the age in years and outputs roughly how many days that is. Use 365 days per year. For 2 years it shows **That is about 730 days.**

hints: First the two scanner lines, then the question and the input, then the calculation, then the output.
`int years = scanner.nextInt();` reads. `int days = years * 365;` calculates, and `System.out.println("That is about " + days + " days.");` outputs.

items.text: I can explain the IPO model.
I can write an input with a data type, a name and a question.
I can join text and variables in an output with +.
I calculate in a variable before the output.
I can pick out input, process and output from a task.
I can read numbers in Java with the scanner.

questions.question: What does IPO stand for?
questions.explanation: Many programs first ask for values, process them and then show the result.

questions.question: The variables a and b have the values 3 and 4. What does `output: a + b` show?
questions.explanation: In an output, + joins the parts together. Calculate the sum in a variable first.

questions.question: Which input fits if a price such as 4.99 should be typed in?
questions.explanation: 4.99 is a decimal number, so double. Also, every input needs a variable name.

questions.question: What does `output: "Age: " + age` show if age has the value 12?
Task: *The program asks for the radius of a circle and shows its circumference.* Match each part of the text to where it belongs in the IPO model.
questions.explanation: The radius is given, the circumference is what you are looking for. The formula connects the two.

questions.question: What does `scanner.nextInt()` read?
questions.explanation: For decimal numbers there is `scanner.nextDouble()`, for a word `scanner.next()`.

lessons.title: Simulation and desk check
lessons.summary: Run a structure chart step by step, work it out by hand and find mistakes.

blocks.text: Before branches and loops come along, you get to know your most important tool. From now on you can use the simulation to check every exercise yourself.

With the ▶︎ Simulation button on the right of the tools, VisuStruct runs your structure chart. While the simulation is running, you cannot edit the diagram. With the pencil icon in the same place you go back to editing.
On the right, the **Controls** appear:

items: **Play** runs the diagram automatically, step by step. You set how long it waits between two steps under **Pause per step**.
**Pause** stops for a moment. Then you carry on with Play or Step.
**Step** runs exactly one step. That way you can watch calmly.
**Stop** cancels and resets everything to the start.

blocks.text: Open the following diagram in the editor and go through it with **Step**:

blocks.caption: The values of a and b are swapped. The variable temp keeps one value meanwhile.

items: **Highlight:** One box in the diagram is coloured. With **Last step** it is the box that has just run. With **Next step** it is the box that comes next.
**Input:** If the diagram asks for a value, you type it in here and confirm with **OK**.

**Last Step:** Here you see what has just happened, e.g. `a = 5 -> 5` after the box `a = b`. On the left, the variables have already been replaced by their values; to the right of the arrow is the result.
**Variables:** All variables with their current values.
**Output:** Everything that was output with `output:`.

blocks.text: If the Programming area is open on the right, the console runs along there as well. It is cleared at the start and then shows output and input just as they would appear in the real program.
At the end, **Simulation finished.** appears. If something goes wrong, the simulation stops on the faulty box and shows a message, e.g. **Unknown variable: total**.

In a **desk check** you play the computer yourself. You go through the structure chart with pen and paper and write down the values of the variables after every step. It is best to make a table: one column for the step, one for each variable and one for the output.
For the diagram above, the table looks like this:
Then compare your table with the simulation. Do the values under **Variables** match your row after every step?
A desk check is especially useful in tests. There you have no computer, but you can still show what your structure chart does.
If a structure chart outputs something wrong, do this:

items: **Write down what you expect:** What should come out for a particular input?
**Run it step by step:** Start the simulation with **Step** and watch the variables.
**Find the spot:** Where does a value first differ from what you expected? That is exactly where the mistake is.

blocks.text: Common mistakes in a sequence are:

items: The **order** is wrong: a variable is used before it has a value.
A value is **overwritten** before it is needed.
**Brackets** are missing: `a + b / 2` is not the same as `(a + b) / 2`.
Two whole numbers are divided: `7 / 2` gives `3`, because with `int` everything after the decimal point is dropped.

blocks.text: Later, branches and loops come along. Then the simulation also shows you which path is taken and how often a loop runs.

exercise.title: Fix the swap

task.text: The structure chart should read in two numbers and output them swapped. So with 3 and 5, first **5** and then **3** should appear. But it outputs 5 twice. Do a desk check or use **Step** and fix the mistake.

hints: Go through the diagram with **Step** and write down the values of a and b after every step. Where does the 3 disappear?
Look at a after the step `a = b`. Where did the old value of a go? Keep it in a temporary variable first, as in the example above.

exercise.title: Fix the cinema tickets

task.text: A cinema ticket costs 8.50 euros. The structure chart should ask for the number of tickets and output the total price, so for 2 tickets `Total: 17.0`. Start the simulation. It stops with an error message. Find out why and fix the structure chart.

hints: Read the error message of the simulation carefully. Which variable does it not know yet?
The simulation runs the boxes from top to bottom. Does total already have a value when the output comes? You can move boxes with the mouse.

blocks.text: If a simulation keeps running forever, click **Stop**. When you **Check** an exercise, VisuStruct stops by itself after a very large number of steps.
You can run Java code step by step too. In the Programming area the tool for this is called the **debugger**:

items: Click a line number on the left. A red dot appears: that is a **breakpoint**. ▶︎ Run pauses before this line.
The Step button runs exactly one line, like **Step** in the simulation.
Below the code you see the current value of every variable. That is your desk check, except that the computer writes it down for you.

exercise.title: Fix the pizza order

task.text: A pizza costs 8 euros, extra cheese 2 euros. For 3 pizzas with extra cheese the program should output **Total: 30**. But it outputs 14. Go through the Java code with Step and watch `total`. Find the mistake and fix it in the code.

hints: What value is in `total` after the fourth line? Work out in your head what Java calculates first.
As in maths, multiplication comes before addition: `price + cheese * count` is `8 + 6`. Add brackets: `(price + cheese) * count`.

items.text: I can start the simulation, pause it, run single steps and stop it.
During the simulation I can read the variables, the output and the last step.
I can do a desk check by hand as a table.
I can find a mistake by comparing the values with what I expect.
I can follow Java code with Step.

questions.question: Which button runs exactly one step?
questions.explanation: Play keeps going automatically, Step runs only one step.

questions.question: What do you write down after every step in a desk check?

options.text: Only the output at the end
The current values of all variables

questions.explanation: That way you see exactly where a value is different from what you expected.

questions.question: First `int a = 3`, then `int b = 5`, then `a = b`. What values do a and b have afterwards?
questions.explanation: The old value of a has been overwritten. That is why you need a temporary variable when swapping.

questions.question: The Last Step field shows `price = 4 * 2.5 -> 10.0`. What does that mean?

options.text: The variable price now has the value 4.
4 * 2.5 was worked out and the result 10.0 was stored in price.
The simulation has found a mistake.

questions.question: The simulation reports **Unknown variable: sum**. What is a likely reason?

options.text: sum is used before it has been given a value.
The structure chart has too many boxes.

questions.question: What does a red dot in front of a line number in the Programming area do?

options.text: The program pauses before this line.

questions.explanation: That is a breakpoint. ▶︎ or Step carries on.

lessons.title: Branch
lessons.summary: Use a condition to decide which of two paths runs.

blocks.text: So far every box always ran. But often a program should **decide**: if a condition is met, do one thing, otherwise do the other.
That is what the **branch** is for. The condition sits in the triangle at the top. Below it, the structure chart splits into two paths:

items: **true** (left): runs if the condition is true
**false** (right): runs if the condition is false

blocks.text: Always **exactly one** of the two paths runs. After that, the program continues below the branch.

blocks.caption: Depending on the age typed in, one message or the other appears. Try 17 and 18 in the simulation.

blocks.text: Drag the **Branch** from the Elements area into the structure chart. Click the triangle and type the condition in the Object Inspector, e.g. `age >= 18`. The word `if` is already in front.
Each path starts with a placeholder ø. Drag statements into it. A path may also hold several boxes on top of each other.
A condition is usually a **comparison**. Its result is always `true` or `false`.

items: `==` equal, e.g. `number == 0`
`!=` not equal, e.g. `answer != 42`
`<` less than, `<=` less than or equal
`>` greater than, `>=` greater than or equal

blocks.text: Do not mix up `==` and `=`. A single `=` is an assignment and stores a value. To compare, you need two equals signs.
With `%` you check whether a number can be divided by another: `number % 2 == 0` is true if `number` is even.

exercise.title: Even or odd

task.text: Ask for a whole number. Output **even** if it is even, otherwise **odd**.

hints: There are two possibilities here, so you need a branch. How do you recognise an even number?
A number is even if there is no remainder when you divide it by 2. The condition is `number % 2 == 0`.

exercise.title: The larger number

task.text: Ask for two whole numbers and output only the larger one. If both are the same, output that number.

hints: A branch compares the two numbers. Each path holds exactly one output.
Compare with `a > b`. In the true path you output `a`, in the false path `b`.

blocks.text: Sometimes something should only happen if the condition is true, and otherwise nothing at all. Then the false path stays **empty**. In the structure chart it shows the placeholder **ø**.

blocks.caption: From 50 euros on, you get 5 euros off. Otherwise nothing happens; the false path is empty. The output below runs in both cases.

exercise.title: Absolute value of a number

task.text: Ask for a whole number. If it is negative, make it positive. Then output the number. So -5 becomes 5, and 7 stays 7. Use a branch with an empty path and only **one** output below the branch.

hints: Only negative numbers need to be changed. What happens to a number if you multiply it by -1?
The condition is `number < 0`. In the true path you flip the sign, e.g. with `number = 0 - number`. The false path stays empty.

blocks.text: This is the age check from the start of this lesson in Java:

items: The condition comes after `if` in **round brackets** `( )`.
The true branch is in **curly brackets** `{ }`, the false branch follows after `else` in its own curly brackets. There is no semicolon after a curly bracket.
If the false branch is empty, simply leave out `else { }`.
Your program needs the first two lines once as soon as it reads input. After that, `scanner.nextInt()` reads a whole number. The question before it is a normal output.

exercise.title: Passed in Java

task.text: Write a Java program that asks for the number of points. From 50 points on it outputs **passed**, otherwise **not passed**. Type the code in the Programming area and then click Check.

hints: Start with the two lines for the scanner. Then ask for the points, read them and compare them with `if`.
The condition is `points >= 50`. One branch has `System.out.println("passed");`, and after `else` comes `System.out.println("not passed");`.

items.text: I know that exactly one path of a branch runs.
I know the comparison operators == != < <= > >=.
I can tell == and = apart.
I can build a branch with an empty path.
I can write a branch with if and else in Java.

questions.question: Which path runs if the condition is false?
questions.explanation: With false, the right path runs. After that, the program continues below the branch.

questions.question: Which condition checks whether age is exactly 18?
questions.explanation: A single = is an assignment. To compare, you need ==.

questions.question: What does ø in a path mean?
The condition is `points >= 50`. For which value is it true?
questions.explanation: >= means greater than or equal. So 50 is included.

questions.question: In textbooks the branch often has another name. Which one?
questions.explanation: The statements in a path only run under a condition. That is why it is also called a conditional statement.

questions.question: Where does the condition of a branch go in Java?

options.text: In round brackets right after if

questions.explanation: `if (age >= 18) { … }`: the round brackets belong to the condition, the curly ones to the branch.

lessons.title: Combining conditions
lessons.summary: Join several conditions with and, or and not, and check ranges of values.

blocks.text: Sometimes a single comparison is not enough. For example, you only get a youth ticket if you are **at least 12 and younger than 18**.
With `&&` (and) you join two conditions. The result is only `true` if **both** conditions are true.

blocks.caption: Both comparisons must be right. Try 11, 12, 17 and 18 in the simulation.

blocks.text: With `||` (or) the result is `true` if **at least one** of the conditions is true. Both may be true as well.
day == 6 || day == 7
This condition is true if `day` has the value 6 or the value 7, so on Saturday or Sunday.
On many keyboards you type the vertical bar `|` with Shift and the backslash key. On a German keyboard it is AltGr and `<`, on a Mac Option and 7.

exercise.title: Weekend

task.text: Ask for a day of the week as a number (1 is Monday, 7 is Sunday). Output **Weekend** if it is Saturday or Sunday, otherwise **Weekday**.

hints: It is the weekend if the day is 6 **or** 7. For that you need two comparisons in one condition.
Saturday is 6, Sunday is 7. Join the two comparisons with `||`.

blocks.text: In German schools, grades go from 1 (best) to 6. You check whether a grade is **in the range** with two comparisons and `&&`:
grade >= 1 && grade <= 6

blocks.caption: The green range from 1 to 6 is valid; both ends are included.

blocks.text: The other way round, a grade is **outside** the range if it is too small **or** too big:

blocks.caption: There is no grade smaller than 1 or bigger than 6.

blocks.text: The way you write it in maths, `1 <= grade <= 6`, does not work. You have to split it into two comparisons and join them with `&&`.

exercise.title: Valid grade

task.text: Ask for a grade as a whole number. Output **valid** if it is between 1 and 6 (1 and 6 are included), otherwise **invalid**.

hints: A valid grade has to meet two things at once: not too small **and** not too big.
The grade must be greater than or equal to 1 and at the same time less than or equal to 6.

blocks.text: With `!` (not) you turn a condition round: `true` becomes `false` and the other way round.
!(grade >= 1 && grade <= 6)
This is true if the grade is **not** in the range, and it means the same as `grade < 1 || grade > 6`.
If `&&` and `||` appear together, `&&` is worked out first, just like multiplication before addition. It is better to use **brackets**; then it is clear what belongs together:
(age >= 12 && age < 18) || student == 1
A **truth table** shows at a glance what `&&`, `||` and `!` produce. On the left are all four possibilities for two conditions `a` and `b`, on the right the result:

blocks.caption: Green is true, red is false. With && there is only one green row, with || only one red one.

blocks.text: Rules of thumb:

items: `a && b` is only true if **both** are true.
`a || b` is only false if **both** are false.
`!a` flips the value.

blocks.text: The result of a condition is a **truth value** of type `boolean`. You can store it in a variable just like a number and use it later:
boolean weekend = day == 6 || day == 7
The branch then only says `weekend`. That reads almost like a sentence: "If weekend, then …". Don't write `weekend == true`, because `weekend` already is true or false.
With `!weekend` you ask for the opposite, a weekday.
Long conditions become clearer when you put parts of them into boolean variables with meaningful names, for example `boolean teenager = age >= 12 && age < 18`.
Now it's your turn. Work out each condition in your head. After every answer you see how VisuStruct evaluates it step by step.

exercise.title: Leap year

task.text: A year is a leap year if it can be divided by 4 but not by 100. Years that can be divided by 400 are leap years anyway. Ask for a year and output **Leap year** or **Not a leap year**.

hints: Check the rule with examples first: 2024 is a leap year, 1900 is not, 2000 is. “Can be divided” means the remainder is 0.
Divisible by 4 means `year % 4 == 0`, not divisible by 100 means `year % 100 != 0`. Join these two with `&&`, put brackets around them and add the case for 400 with `||`.

blocks.text: The youth ticket from the start looks like this in Java:
The symbols `&&`, `||` and `!` are exactly the ones you already use in the structure chart. They come from Java. As always, the whole condition is in the round brackets after `if`.

exercise.title: School or free time

task.text: Write a Java program that asks for the hour (0 to 23). From 8 up to and including 15 it outputs **School**, otherwise **Free time**.

hints: The hour has to meet two conditions at the same time. Which operator means “and”?
`if (hour >= 8 && hour <= 15) { … } else { … }`

items.text: I know when a combination with && is true.
I know when a combination with || is true.
I can turn a condition round with !.
I can check whether a value is in a range such as 1 to 6.
I can read the truth table for &&, || and !.
I can store the result of a condition in a boolean variable.
I got at least 8 of 10 conditions right in the game.
I can combine conditions in Java with && and ||.

questions.question: When is `a && b` true?

options.text: If a or b is true
Only if a and b are both true
If exactly one of them is true

questions.explanation: With && both parts must be right. If one is false, the whole thing is false.

questions.question: The variable day has the value 6. What does `day == 6 || day == 7` give?
questions.explanation: With || it is enough if one side is true.

questions.question: Which condition checks whether number is between 10 and 20 (both included)?
questions.explanation: With || every number would be allowed, because every number is greater than 10 or less than 20.

questions.question: What does `!(5 > 3)` give?
questions.explanation: 5 > 3 is true, and ! turns that round.

questions.question: How do you write “age is at least 12 and less than 18” in Java?
questions.explanation: Each comparison stands on its own, joined with `&&`.

lessons.title: Switch
lessons.summary: Run one of many cases, depending on the value of a variable.

blocks.text: A drinks machine has three buttons: 1 for water, 2 for juice, 3 for cocoa. With branches you need three boxes nested inside each other. That quickly gets wide and confusing.

blocks.caption: The machine with three nested branches. Each branch checks the same variable choice again.

blocks.text: Whenever you compare **one variable** with **several fixed values**, there is an easier way: the **switch**.
At the top of the box is the variable that decides. Below it there is a column of its own for every case. Above each column is the value it belongs to.

blocks.caption: The same machine as a switch. If choice has the value 2, only column 2 runs.

items: The simulation looks for the case whose name matches the value exactly.
If no case matches, **default** runs. This case is always on the far right.
After that, the program continues below the switch. Only **one** case ever runs.

blocks.text: A new switch has the cases 1, 2 and default. Click a case to change its **Case name** in the Object Inspector. With **Add Case** you get a new column in front of default.
The cases do not have to be numbers. You can also choose by the content of a `String` variable. Then you write the text as the case name, for example `red`.

blocks.caption: A traffic light: depending on the colour typed in, a different message appears. In the simulation, also try a colour that does not exist.

blocks.text: Upper and lower case matter: `Red` does not match the case `red`.

exercise.title: Grade in words

task.text: Ask for a grade as a whole number and output it in words: 1 very good, 2 good, 3 satisfactory, 4 sufficient, 5 poor, 6 fail. For any other number, **Not a valid grade** should appear.

hints: For many fixed values, a switch is clearer than lots of branches. Every grade gets a case of its own.
Keep using “Add Case” until you have the cases 1 to 6 and default. At the top of the switch you write `grade`.

exercise.title: Calculator

task.text: Ask, one after another, for a whole number `a`, an operator as a `String` and a second whole number `b`. For `+`, `-` and `*` you output the result. For any other sign, **Unknown operator** appears.

hints: First read in all three values. After that, a switch on the operator decides what is calculated.
Before the switch, create `int result = 0`. In each case you calculate, for example, `result = a + b` and then output `result`. The case names are simply `+`, `-` and `*`.

blocks.text: The switch only checks whether a value is **exactly equal** to a case name. So:

items: **Switch:** one variable, several fixed values. Examples: choosing from a menu, day of the week as a number, grades.
**Branch:** ranges and combined conditions. Examples: `age >= 18`, `temperature < 0 || temperature > 30`.

blocks.text: So for “age 18 or older” you still need the branch. You cannot create a case of its own for every possible age.
The drinks machine looks like this in Java:

items: After `switch`, the variable being compared is in round brackets.
Every case starts with `case`, the value and an arrow `->`. After it, curly brackets hold what should happen.
`default` is the otherwise case. It runs when no value matches.

exercise.title: Dice in words

task.text: Write a Java program with `switch` that reads a number. For 1 it outputs **one**, for 2 **two**, for 3 **three** and otherwise **unknown**.

hints: You need three `case` branches and one `default` branch.
`switch (number) { case 1 -> { System.out.println("one"); } … default -> { System.out.println("unknown"); } }`

items.text: I can insert a switch, add cases and change case names.
I know when the case default runs.
I can decide whether a switch or a branch fits better.
I can write a case selection in Java with switch.

questions.question: The variable day has the value 5. There are the cases 1, 2, 3 and default. What runs?
questions.explanation: No case name matches 5, so default applies.

questions.question: How many cases run each time the switch runs?

options.text: All cases from the matching one on

questions.explanation: After the matching case, the program continues straight below the switch.

questions.question: What is a switch NOT suitable for?

options.text: Checking whether a temperature is above 30 degrees
Handling a colour such as red, yellow or green

questions.explanation: “Above 30” is a range. For that you need a branch with a comparison.

lessons.title: While loop
lessons.summary: Repeat steps as long as a condition is true.

steps.title: Repeat as long as something holds

blocks.text: Often a program should do something several times. Instead of writing the same box five times, you use a **loop**.
The **while loop** repeats its inside **as long as** its condition is true. The condition is at the top, in the head of the box. The inside is indented below it, framed by a bracket on the left.

blocks.caption: A countdown: as long as number is greater than 0, number is output and gets smaller by 1. After that, Start! appears.

blocks.text: The while loop is a **pre-test loop**. Before **every** pass, the condition is checked:

items: Check the condition.
If it is true, run the inside once and start again at 1.
If it is false, the program continues below the loop.

blocks.caption: After every pass it goes back to the condition. Only when it is false does the program continue below the loop.

blocks.text: In the countdown the condition is checked four times: with 3, 2 and 1 it is true, with 0 it is false.
If the condition is already false the first time it is checked, the inside runs **not even once**. Start the countdown with `int number = 0` and only Start! appears.
Many loops count along. For that you need three things:

items: **A start value before the loop**, e.g. `int i = 1`
**A condition in the head**, e.g. `i <= 5`
**A change inside**, e.g. `i = i + 1` (short: `i++`)

blocks.text: If one of these parts is missing, the loop counts wrongly or not at all.

Counting loops are ancient! In their 1973 article, Nassi and Shneiderman showed their idea using the **factorial**, among other things: 5! = 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 = 120. Here is my goat version of it. Try it with **Step** in the simulation and watch `factorial` grow. Baaah, that goes fast!

blocks.caption: The factorial with a counter variable `i`, rebuilt from an example in the 1973 article.

exercise.title: Count to n

task.text: Ask for a whole number `n` and output all numbers from 1 to `n`, each on its own line.

hints: You need a counter variable that starts at 1 and grows by 1 in every pass.
Before the loop, create `int i = 1`. The condition is `i <= n`. Inside, you output `i` and then increase `i` by 1.

blocks.text: If nothing inside the loop changes the condition, it stays true forever. The loop never stops. This is called an **endless loop**.

blocks.caption: Here number = number - 1 is missing. The loop outputs 3 again and again and never reaches Start!

blocks.text: Ask yourself for every loop: **What inside makes sure that the condition becomes false at some point?** When an exercise is checked, VisuStruct stops after a very large number of steps and reports a possible endless loop.

exercise.title: Double up to 100

task.text: Ask for a whole number. Keep doubling it until it is at least 100. At the end, output **how often** you doubled it.

hints: The loop runs as long as the number is still too small. Count along how often it has run.

You need a second variable `int steps = 0`. The condition is `number < 100`. Inside, you double the number with `number = number * 2` and increase `steps` by 1. If the number is already 100, the loop does not run at all.

blocks.text: With a loop, the **desk check** is especially valuable. You see exactly how often the loop runs and with which value it stops. Every check of the condition gets a row of its own.

blocks.caption: A while loop adds up the numbers 1, 2 and 3.

blocks.text: Common mistakes in loops are:

items: The loop runs **once too often or once too few**, e.g. `<` instead of `<=`.
A variable is **not changed** in the loop, or changed in the wrong direction. Then the loop never ends.
A variable gets its start value **inside** the loop instead of before it and is reset in every pass.

exercise.title: Fix the countdown

task.text: The countdown should count down from the start value and output **Go!** at the end. So with 3: 3, 2, 1, Go! The start diagram has two mistakes. Find and fix both.

hints: There are two mistakes. One is about counting, the other about the output at the end.
Start the simulation with start value 3 and watch i under Variables. Does i get smaller? Also compare the last output carefully with the task.

blocks.text: The countdown from the start of this lesson looks like this in Java:

items: After `while` the condition is in round brackets, as with `if`.
Everything that is repeated is in curly brackets. That is the body of the loop.
The body is indented. As in the structure chart, you can see what belongs to the loop.

exercise.title: Even numbers in Java

task.text: Write a Java program that reads a whole number `n` and uses a while loop to output all even numbers from 2 up to at most `n`. For 7 that is 2, 4 and 6.

hints: You need a counter variable that starts at 2. The loop runs as long as it is not greater than `n`.
`int number = 2;` before the loop, then `while (number <= n) { … }`. In the body you output `number` and increase it with `number = number + 2;`.

I can use a counter variable with a start value, a condition and a change.
I notice when a loop never ends and can fix the mistake.
I can follow a loop pass by pass in a desk check.
I can write a while loop in Java.

lessons.title: Do-while loop
lessons.summary: Run first, check afterwards: loops with at least one pass.

blocks.text: The **do-while loop** is a **post-test loop**. The condition is at the bottom, in the foot of the box. This is how it runs:

items: Run the inside once.
Check the condition.
If it is true, start again at 1. If it is false, the program continues below the loop.

blocks.caption: On the left, the while loop checks first; on the right, the do-while loop runs first.

blocks.text: At the top of the box is `do`, and the condition is in the foot. When you click the loop, the word `while` is in front of the text field in the Object Inspector: the condition means “repeat as long as …”.
Just like with the while loop, the condition says **when the loop repeats**. As long as it is true, the loop keeps running.
Because the condition is only checked at the end, the inside **always runs at least once**. That is the most important difference from the while loop.

blocks.caption: i is 10 and so it is not less than 5. Still, 10 is output once, because the check only comes afterwards.

blocks.text: With a while loop and the same condition `i < 5`, nothing at all would be output here.
The do-while loop fits whenever something has to happen first before you can check it. The best example is an input: only after someone has typed something do you know whether it is valid.

blocks.caption: The question comes again until a number from 1 to 10 has been typed in. In the simulation, first try 0 and then 12.

blocks.text: Here the condition describes the **invalid** input: `number < 1 || number > 10`. As long as the input is invalid, the question is asked again.

exercise.title: Valid grade

task.text: Ask for a grade. If it is not between 1 and 6, ask again. If it is valid, output it, for example **Your grade: 3**.

hints: The grade is asked for at least once. After that, the condition decides whether to ask again.
Before the loop, create `int grade = 0`. The input `input: grade "Grade from 1 to 6"` goes inside the loop. The condition is `grade < 1 || grade > 6`.

exercise.title: Sum until 0

task.text: Keep asking for numbers until a 0 is typed in. Then output the sum of all the numbers typed in.

hints: You need a variable for the sum that starts at 0 before the loop. In every pass the new number is added.

Before the loop, create `int sum = 0` and `int number = 0`. In the loop you ask for `number` and calculate `sum = sum + number`. Adding the 0 does no harm. The loop keeps running as long as `number != 0`.

blocks.text: The loop that still runs once looks like this in Java:

items: The body is between `do {` and `}`, the condition only comes afterwards.
Here there is a **semicolon** after `while (…)`. That is different from the while loop.

exercise.title: Double at least once

task.text: Write a Java program that reads a start number. A do-while loop doubles it and outputs it as long as it is less than 100. A number of 100 or more is still doubled at least once: 200 becomes 400.

hints: In the body you double the number and output it. The condition comes at the end.
`do { number = number * 2; System.out.println(number); } while (number < 100);`

I know that the inside runs at least once.
I can repeat an input until it is valid.
I can write a do-while loop in Java.

questions.question: What does post-test loop mean?

options.text: The condition is checked before every pass.
The condition is checked after every pass.

questions.question: You want to ask for a number from 1 to 10. Which condition goes in the foot?

questions.question: When is a do-while loop better than a while loop?

When the loop might not need to run at all
When you want to count exactly to 10

lessons.title: For loop
lessons.summary: Count a fixed number of passes with Init, Condition and Step.

blocks.text: In the while loop you already counted along: a start value before the loop, a condition in the head, a change inside. The **for loop** puts these three parts together in the head. That way you see at a glance how it counts.
When you click a for loop, it has three fields on the right:

items: **Init:** `int i = 1` creates the counter variable.
**Condition:** `i <= 5` says how long to count.
**Step:** `i++` increases `i` by 1 after every pass.

blocks.caption: A for loop that outputs the numbers from 1 to 5.

blocks.text: The three parts run at different times:

items: **Init** runs exactly once, right at the start.
**Condition** is checked before every pass. If it is false, the loop is finished.
After the inside comes the **Step**, then the condition again.

blocks.caption: Init only runs once. After that, condition, inside and step repeat.

blocks.text: So the for loop is a pre-test loop, like the while loop. Go through the example in the simulation with **Step** and watch how `i` changes.

Use the for loop when you know beforehand how often something should happen. If the end depends on something that only happens during the loop, for example an input, the while or do-while loop is better.
A for loop is good for adding up numbers. Before the loop there is `int sum = 0`. In every pass the current number `i` is added.

blocks.caption: With n = 4 the loop calculates 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. At the end, 10 is output.

blocks.text: The step does not always have to be `i++`:

items: `i--` counts backwards, for example with Init `int i = 10` and Condition `i >= 1`.
`i = i + 2` jumps in steps of two, for example 0, 2, 4, 6.

blocks.text: Make sure that Init, Condition and Step fit together. With Init `int i = 1`, Condition `i >= 1` and Step `i++`, the condition never becomes false.

exercise.title: Countdown

task.text: Ask for a whole number `n`. Use a for loop to count backwards from `n` to 1 and output each number. Then output **Go!**.

hints: This time the for loop counts backwards. Think about where it starts, when it stops and how it counts.
Init is `int i = n`, the condition `i >= 1` and the step `i--`. The output Go! goes below the loop, not inside it.

hints: The loop counts from 1 to 10. In every pass you output one line of the table.
Inside, first calculate `int product = number * i`. Then output `number + " x " + i + " = " + product`. Remember the spaces inside the quotation marks.

task.text: The structure chart should add up all numbers from 1 to n. So with n = 4 the result should be 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = **10**. But it outputs 6. Do a desk check or use **Step** and fix the mistake.

lessons.title: Nesting
lessons.summary: Combine branches inside loops and loops inside loops.

blocks.text: You now know all the important building blocks: sequence, branch, switch and three kinds of loops. They only get really powerful together.
Every path and every loop body is a sequence itself. You may put any element there, including more branches and loops. This is called **nesting**.
To do this, simply drag an element onto the placeholder ø inside a loop or a path.
The loop goes through all the numbers, and the branch decides for each single number whether something happens. That way you can count, for example, how many even numbers there are from 1 to n.

blocks.caption: In every pass the branch checks with i % 2 == 0 whether i is even. Only then is count increased by 1. The false path stays empty.

blocks.text: With n = 7 these are the numbers 2, 4 and 6, so 3 is output.

exercise.title: Count even inputs

task.text: Ask for exactly **five** whole numbers, one after another. Then output how many of them were even.

hints: Doing the same thing five times means: loop. In every pass a number is read in and checked.
A for loop from 1 to 5. Inside, first comes the input `input: int number "Enter a number"`, below it a branch with `number % 2 == 0`. In the true path you increase `count` by 1.

blocks.text: If one loop sits inside another, the **inner loop runs all the way through in every pass of the outer one**. With this you can build patterns of rows and columns.

blocks.caption: The outer loop counts the lines. The inner one adds as many stars to the text as the line number says. With n = 3 you get a triangle of 1, 2 and 3 stars.

blocks.text: With `String text = ""` every line starts empty. `text = text + "*"` adds a star. Only when the line is finished is it output.

hints: You need two loops inside each other: one for the lines and inside it one for the characters of a line.
Build it like the triangle. The difference: the inner loop always counts up to `width`, not up to the line number. The outer loop counts up to `height`.

blocks.text: With nested diagrams, the drawing helps you: whatever is further inside is indented and surrounded by its loop or path.

items: Read from the outside in: what repeats? What is decided in every pass?
Give counter variables meaningful names such as `line` and `column`. Two loops must not change the same counter variable.
Go through an example in the simulation with **Step** and watch the variables.

blocks.text: This is exactly what the structure chart was invented for. Shneiderman asked himself: if we are supposed to do without GOTO, why not do without the arrows in the flowchart as well? The result: no arrow spaghetti, and every block stays nicely in its pen. [The whole story](https://visustruct.org/en/angeberwissen.html)

What is nested in the structure chart is nested in curly brackets in Java. Every level is indented four spaces further. If your code gets messy, the **Indent** button at the top of the Programming area helps.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: Store many values under one name, reach them with the index and go through them with a loop.

blocks.text: Imagine you want to store the points from five tests. With five variables `points1` to `points5` that quickly gets confusing. An **array** is a row of slots that all have the same name and the same data type.
You create an array with a statement. After the data type you write square brackets `[]`:

int[] numbers = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}
String[] names = {"Ada", "Ben", "Cem"}
The values in the curly brackets go straight into the slots. You can also create an empty array with a fixed number of slots:

int[] points = new int[5]
String[] names = new String[3]
With `new int[5]` all five slots hold zeros at first, with `new String[3]` empty texts.
Every slot has a number, the **index**. Counting starts at **0**. So with `int[] numbers = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}`:

items: `numbers[0]` is 2
`numbers[1]` is 4
`numbers[4]` is 10

blocks.caption: Five slots with the indices 0 to 4. The index is above the slot, the value inside it.

blocks.text: **Why start at 0?** In computer science the index is not “which slot” but the **distance from the start**. The first slot is right at the start, so 0 steps away. The second is 1 step away, the third 2 steps. You know this from a lift: the ground floor is **0**, and the first floor is one level above it.
This gives you a rule worth remembering: with 5 slots the **last index is 4**, always one less than the number of slots.

Counting from 0 is pretty old. The programming language C from 1972 already works like this: the computer knows the address of the first slot, and for `numbers[i]` it simply calculates “start plus i slots further”. With i = 0 it stays at the start, which saves a calculation. Java, Python and JavaScript took this over. By the way, I count my horns from 0 as well: horn 0 on the left, horn 1 on the right.
With the index you read a value or write a new one into it:

output: numbers[0]
numbers[1] = 99
An array with 5 slots has the indices 0 to 4. `numbers[5]` does not exist. The simulation then reports an invalid expression.
`numbers.length` tells you how many slots an array has. With five values it is 5. So the **last** index is always `numbers.length - 1`:

output: numbers.length
output: numbers[numbers.length - 1]
The second line outputs the last value, however long the array is. VisuStruct also understands `numbers.length()`.

exercise.title: First and last value

task.text: Create the array `int[] values = {4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42}`. Then output on three lines: the first value, the last value and the number of values. For the last value, use the length and do not simply write the index 5.

hints: Counting starts at 0, so the first slot has the index 0. And what is the index of the last slot?
The first value is `values[0]`. The last one is `values[values.length - 1]`. The number of values is `values.length`.

steps.title: Go through an array with a loop

blocks.text: An array shows its strength together with a **for loop**. The counter variable `i` runs from 0 to the last index and is used as the index:

int i = 0
i < numbers.length
i++
In the first pass `i` is 0, in the last one 4. Because the condition is `i < numbers.length`, the loop fits any length.

blocks.caption: The for loop outputs all five values one after another. Under Variables in the simulation, watch i count from 0 to 4.

blocks.text: This is also how you fill an empty array with inputs. As the target of the input you write the slot `names[i]`:

blocks.caption: Three names are asked for and written into the slots 0, 1 and 2.

hints: You need two loops: one for reading in from front to back and one for outputting from back to front.

You create the array with `int[] numbers = new int[4]`. The input is `input: numbers[i] "Enter a number"`. For the second loop you start at `int i = numbers.length - 1`, check `i >= 0` and count down with `i--`.

items: **Sum:** You start with `sum = 0` and add every value in the loop.
**Maximum:** First you remember the value in slot 0 as the largest so far. In the loop you check every value. If it is larger, it becomes the new maximum.
