lessons.title: Two-dimensional arrays
lessons.summary: Store values in rows and columns, like the seats in a cinema, and go through them with two nested loops.

blocks.text: A cinema has several **rows**, and every row has several **seats**. For every seat we want to remember whether its ticket has already been sold. That is a yes-or-no question, so the data type `boolean` fits: `true` means sold, `false` means free.

A normal array is one single row of slots. For the cinema we need a **table** with rows and columns. That is a **two-dimensional array**, 2D array for short. You write two pairs of square brackets for it:
boolean[][] seats = new boolean[3][5]
That gives 3 rows with 5 seats each, so 15 slots. At the start every slot holds `false`: all seats are free.

blocks.caption: The first index is the row, the second the seat. Both are counted from 0.

blocks.text: For a slot you now need **two** indices: first the row, then the seat.
seats[1][2] = true
Now seat 2 in row 1 is sold. Reading works the same way: `seats[1][2]` is now `true`.
You can also ask for the size:

items: `seats.length` is the number of **rows**, here 3.
`seats[0].length` is the number of **seats** in row 0, here 5.

blocks.caption: Three tickets are sold. After that, the diagram outputs the size of the cinema and whether row 1, seat 2 is sold. Watch under Variables in the simulation: seats is shown row by row.

blocks.text: Just like with a normal array, there is no slot `seats[3][0]`, because the rows are called 0, 1 and 2. The simulation then reports an invalid expression.
To look at **all** seats, you need two for loops inside each other:

items: The **outer loop** counts the row: `row` runs from 0 to 2.
The **inner loop** counts the seat: `seat` runs from 0 to 4.

blocks.caption: Blue is the outer loop, orange the inner one. The numbers show the order in which the seats come up.

blocks.text: For every row, the inner loop runs **all the way** through once. Only when `seat` has visited all five seats does the outer loop move `row` on by one. Then `seat` starts at 0 again. That way all 3 · 5 = 15 seats come up exactly once.
The conditions are `row < seats.length` and `seat < seats[row].length`. That way the loops fit a cinema of any size.

blocks.caption: The seating plan: for every row, a line of X (sold) and O (free) is put together and output. Go through it with Step and watch how seat keeps starting again from the beginning while row only slowly counts on.

blocks.text: Every phone photo is a 2D array! A photo with 4000 · 3000 pixels has 3000 rows with 4000 slots each, so 12 million pixels. Every slot holds the colour of one dot. When you make a photo brighter, the phone runs over all the pixels with two nested loops. My profile picture, by the way, has only one slot: brown.

exercise.title: Count free seats

task.text: In the start diagram three tickets have already been sold. Use two nested loops to count how many seats are still **free**, and output e.g. `Free: 12`.

hints: Just like for the seating plan, you go over all seats with two loops. Instead of outputting something, you count.
Before the loops, create `int free = 0`. A seat is free if `seats[row][seat]` is false. The condition for that is `!seats[row][seat]`.

exercise.title: Sell a ticket

task.text: The start diagram asks for a row and a seat. If the seat is already sold, output `Already sold`. Otherwise mark it as sold and output e.g. `Sold: row 0, seat 4`.

hints: First check whether the seat is sold. Depending on the answer, something different happens.
You do not need a loop here. A branch with the condition `seats[row][seat]` is enough. In the false path you set the slot to `true`.

exercise.title: Times table grid

task.text: Create `int[][] table = new int[10][10]` and fill it with the times tables up to 10 using two loops. Then ask for two numbers from 1 to 10 and read the result from the table, e.g. `3 · 4 = 12`.

hints: First two nested loops fill the table; after that you read only one single slot.
The indices run from 0 to 9, but the numbers from 1 to 10. That is why the slot `table[i][j]` holds the value `(i + 1) * (j + 1)`, and for 3 · 4 you read `table[a - 1][b - 1]`.

blocks.text: The cinema looks like this in Java:

items: Two pairs of square brackets `[][]` stand for a table: first the row, then the seat.
`seats.length` is the number of rows, `seats[0].length` the number of seats in one row.
With fixed values you write every row in its own curly brackets: `int[][] t = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}};`

exercise.title: Add up the points

task.text: Three players have played two rounds each. Create the table `points` in Java with the rows {3, 5}, {4, 1} and {2, 2}. Add up all points with two nested for loops and output **Sum: 17**.

hints: The outer loop goes through the rows, the inner one through the seats of a row.
`int[][] points = {{3, 5}, {4, 1}, {2, 2}};` and in the inner loop `sum = sum + points[i][j];`. The inner loop runs up to `points[i].length`.

items.text: I can create a 2D array and know what the two numbers mean.
I can read and write a slot with a row and a seat.
I know the difference between `seats.length` and `seats[0].length`.
I can explain in which order two nested loops visit the slots.
I can create and go through a two-dimensional array in Java.

questions.question: How many slots does `boolean[][] seats = new boolean[4][6]` have?
questions.explanation: 4 rows with 6 seats each: 4 · 6 = 24.

questions.question: What is in all slots after `new boolean[3][5]`?
questions.explanation: A new boolean array is filled with false. In the cinema that means: all seats are free.

questions.question: Two nested loops run over 3 rows with 5 seats. How often does the inside of the **inner** loop run?
questions.explanation: For each of the 3 rows the inner loop runs 5 times: 3 · 5 = 15.

questions.question: Match what each expression means in the cinema.
What does `seats.length` give for `new boolean[3][5]`?

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.summary: Work with text: read single characters, cut out parts, search, compare and split.

steps.title: Text is a row of characters

blocks.text: You already know `String`: `String name = "Ludwig"`. In computer science such a text is called a **string**, because the characters hang one after another like beads on a string. Every character has a place with an index, just like in an array. Here, too, **counting starts at 0**: the first character is 0 steps away from the start.

blocks.caption: The nine characters of “Billygoat” with their indices 0 to 8.

blocks.text: A String comes with **methods**. You write the name of the variable, a dot and the method:

items: `word.length()` gives the number of characters, here 9.
`word.charAt(0)` gives the character with the index 0, here `'B'`.

blocks.text: With Strings you write `length()` **with** brackets, with arrays `length` **without**. Sadly, that is just how Java is.
In Java a single character has the data type `char`. A `char` goes in **single** quotation marks: `'B'`. A String goes in double ones: `"B"`.

char first = word.charAt(0)
char last = word.charAt(word.length() - 1)
Just like in an array, the last character has the index `length() - 1`.
With `substring` you cut a part out of the text:

items: `word.substring(0, 5)` gives the characters from index 0 **up to just before** index 5, so `"Billy"`.
`word.substring(5)` gives everything from index 5 to the end, so `"goat"`.

blocks.text: The end is **not** included. Handy: `substring(0, 5)` gives exactly 5 characters.

blocks.caption: All the methods from this lesson in one example. Go through it in the simulation and compare every output with the picture.

blocks.text: More methods you often need:
In Java you compare two Strings with `equals`, not with `==`. Two single characters (`char`), on the other hand, you compare with `==`, e.g. `word.charAt(i) == 'e'`.

Try `"Billygoat".equals("billygoat")`. The answer is false! For a computer, B and b are completely different characters. Inside, every character is stored as a number: B is 66 and b is 98. This numbering is called ASCII and dates from 1963. Baah, so for a computer Ludwig and ludwig are two different goats. I am the one with the capital L.
With a for loop you go through a text character by character. The index `i` runs from 0 to `word.length() - 1`, just like with an array:

blocks.caption: Counts how often the letter e appears. In the simulation, try “cheese” and watch i and count.

blocks.text: Often several pieces of information sit in one single line, separated by a character, e.g. `"Ludwig;billy goat;7"`. With `split` you cut the line apart at this character. The result is a **String array**:
String[] parts = line.split(";")
After that, `parts[0]` is `"Ludwig"`, `parts[1]` is `"billy goat"` and `parts[2]` is `"7"`. With `parts.length` you find out how many parts there are.

blocks.caption: The line is split at the semicolon, and every part is output with its index.

blocks.text: CSV files, which you know from spreadsheets, are built the same way: one line per record, the values separated by a comma or semicolon.

exercise.title: Initials

task.text: Ask for a first name and a last name and output the initials. So for Ludwig Billygoat that is `L. B.`

hints: The initial is the first letter of a name. Which method gives the character at a particular place?
`firstName.charAt(0)` gives the first letter. The output is then `firstName.charAt(0) + ". " + lastName.charAt(0) + "."`

exercise.title: Backwards

task.text: Ask for a word and output it backwards. Ludwig becomes `giwduL`.

hints: Go through the word character by character, but from back to front, and build a new text as you go.
Create `String backwards = ""`. The loop starts at the last index `word.length() - 1` and counts down to 0 with `i--`. In every pass you add `word.charAt(i)` at the end.

exercise.title: Count words

task.text: Ask for a sentence and output how many words it has, e.g. `Words: 4` for “Ludwig is a goat”. The words are separated by exactly one space.

hints: There is always a space between the words. Which method splits a text at a character?
Split the sentence into a String array with `sentence.split(" ")`. Its length is the number of words.

blocks.text: The methods in this lesson already are Java. A whole program with a text looks like this:

items: `scanner.next()` reads one word, that is text up to the next space. For numbers you keep using `scanner.nextInt()`.
Text goes in **double** quotes `"Ludwig"`, a single character in **single** quotes `'L'`.
`length()`, `toUpperCase()` and the other methods always have round brackets after them, even when nothing is inside.
You compare two texts with `equals`. Every letter counts: `"Ludwig".equals("ludwig")` is false.

exercise.title: Check the password

task.text: Write a Java program that asks for the password. If it is **Ludwig**, it outputs **Welcome!**, otherwise **Wrong password**. Mind upper and lower case: `ludwig` is wrong.

hints: Read the password with `scanner.next()` into a String variable. Then compare it in a selection.
The condition is `input.equals("Ludwig")`. In Java, `==` does not reliably compare texts.

blocks.text: A String can do much more. You will often need these methods too:

head: Method
Meaning
Example
Result
rows: same text, whether upper or lower case?
the text n times in a row
adds text to the end, like `+`
Which comes first in the alphabet?

blocks.text: `compareTo` returns a number: **negative** if the text comes earlier in the alphabet, **0** if both are the same, and **positive** if it comes later. You can use it to sort names.
Two methods do not belong to a text but to a class. That is why the class name comes first:

items: `Integer.parseInt("7")` turns the text "7" into the number 7. You can calculate with it.
`String.valueOf(7)` turns the number 7 into the text "7".

blocks.caption: All the new methods in one example. Go through it in the simulation and compare every output with the table.

blocks.text: Programs often get their text from a **file**. Princess Zora has written Ludwig a letter. It is ready as the file `letter.txt`:

blocks.name: letter.txt
blocks.content:
Dear Ludwig,
the fox has locked me in his tower.
The door has a lock with a secret word.
You can only find the word with Java.
Please help me!
Yours, Princess Zora

blocks.text: These lines read the whole file into a String:

import java.nio.file.*;

String letter = Files.readString(Path.of("letter.txt"));
You will learn exactly how reading works later, in a lesson of its own about files. For now this is enough: afterwards the whole letter is in `letter`, with all its lines.
At the end of every line there is an invisible character for the **line break**. In Java you write it as `"\n"`. So `letter.split("\n")` splits the letter into its lines.

exercise.title: Where is the fox?

task.text: The start code already reads the letter. Split it into lines and output **Lines:** and the number of lines. Then find the line that contains **fox** and output **Fox in line** and its number. The first line has the number 1.

hints: `String[] lines = letter.split("\n");` splits the letter. Then a for loop goes through all the lines.
In the loop you check `lines[i].contains("fox")`. The index starts at 0, so you output `(i + 1)`. You need the brackets so that Java calculates instead of adding 1 to the text.

blocks.text: Nobody knows all methods by heart, not even professionals. They look them up in the **Java API**. API stands for Application Programming Interface. It means the description of everything Java already brings along.
You can find all methods of String here: [String in the Java API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/String.html)
Scroll down to the table **Method Summary**. Each row describes one method:

head: Column
Example
Meaning
rows: Name and parameters with their data type
Returns the index within this string of the last occurrence …

blocks.text: The page is very long. Press Ctrl+F (on a Mac ⌘+F) and search for the name of the method to get there at once.
Look up these methods. They are not in this lesson:

questions.question: Look up `strip()`. What does the method do?

options.text: It removes all spaces in the text.
It removes the spaces at the beginning and the end.
It cuts off the last character.

questions.explanation: Like `trim()`. But `strip()` also knows special spaces from other writing systems.

questions.question: Look up `isBlank()`. What does `"   ".isBlank()` return?
questions.explanation: isBlank checks whether the text is empty or only contains spaces. `"   ".isEmpty()`, on the other hand, would be false.

questions.question: Look up `toCharArray()`. Which data type does the method return?
questions.explanation: An array with all characters of the text, one element for each character.

questions.question: Look up `indexOf` with two parameters. What does `"Billygoat".indexOf("l", 3)` return?
questions.explanation: The search only starts at index 3. The first l from there is at index 3.

questions.question: Look up `startsWith`. Which data type does the method return?
questions.explanation: The column “Modifier and Type” says boolean: the answer is true or false.

blocks.text: Now you help Ludwig. The fox has locked Princess Zora in his tower, and the gate only opens with a secret word.

items.text: I know that the characters of a String are also counted from 0.
I can work with `length()` and `charAt(i)`.
I can cut a part out of a text with `substring`.
I know `indexOf`, `contains`, `toUpperCase` and `equals`.
I can go through a text character by character with a loop.
I can split a text into a String array with `split`.
I can read a text in Java and compare it with `equals`.
I know more methods such as `lastIndexOf`, `replace`, `compareTo` and `Integer.parseInt`.
I can split a text from a file into lines with `split("\n")`.
I can look up a method in the Java API and read its description.

questions.question: What does `"Ludwig".charAt(1)` give?
questions.explanation: Counting starts at 0: L has the index 0, u the index 1.

questions.question: What does `"Structure".substring(0, 6)` give?
questions.explanation: The characters with the indices 0 to 5. The end 6 is not included.

questions.question: A word has 7 characters. Which index does the last character have?
questions.explanation: Just like with an array: always one less than the length.

questions.question: How do you compare two Strings for the same content in Java?
Match each method to what it gives for `"Billygoat"`.
Which condition checks in Java whether `input` contains the text Ludwig?
questions.explanation: You compare texts with equals. Single quotes are only for a single character.

questions.question: What does `Integer.parseInt("12") + 1` return?
questions.explanation: parseInt turns the text into a number. After that Java calculates as usual.

lessons.title: Call and break
lessons.summary: Split big tasks into subprograms and leave loops early.

blocks.text: Long structure charts quickly get confusing. That is why you split a big task into **smaller problems**. Every smaller problem gets a name of its own and a structure chart of its own, a **subprogram**.
A quiz, for example, has three parts: greet, ask questions, show the result. The main program only names these three parts:

blocks.caption: The main program is made of just three calls. What happens in each part is in a structure chart of its own.

blocks.text: That way you see at a glance how the program is built. The details are somewhere else.
A **call** is a box with double vertical lines on the left and right. It means: run the subprogram with this name here, then carry on.

items: You drag **Call** from the Elements area and type the name into it, e.g. `showGreeting()`.
The round brackets at the end show that it is a subprogram. That is how you write it in Java, Python and JavaScript, too.
You build the subprogram itself as a structure chart of its own in a new tab. As the title you type the same name.

blocks.caption: The subprogram showGreeting() as a structure chart of its own.

blocks.text: **In the simulation:** When the simulation reaches a call, it looks among the open tabs for the structure chart with this title and runs it. Then it carries on in the main program. While the subprogram is running, the call box stays highlighted. A subprogram like this one, with only a name as its title, shares its variables with the main program. You will soon learn how a subprogram gets variables of its own. If there is no matching tab, the simulation skips the call and shows a note.

Why does your teacher always say “method” in Java and never “function” or “procedure”? Because in Java every subprogram has to belong to a class, and the subprograms of a class are called methods. The difference still exists, though: if a method hands back a result, it is really a function. If it has `void` in front, it hands back nothing and is really a procedure. Java just keeps it simple and calls both methods. So do I: my method is called Munching.

exercise.title: Greeting with a call

task.text: Imagine the subprogram `showTitle()` already exists. Build the main program: first it calls `showTitle()`. Then it asks for a name and outputs **Hello** and the name. So when Ada is typed in, **Hello Ada** appears.

hints: The main program has three parts: the call, the input and the output.
Drag a Call from the Elements area right to the top and type `showTitle()` into it. Below it come the input `input: String name "What is your name?"` and the output.

blocks.text: Often a subprogram should work with values that are only known when it is called. Then it gets a **header line** as its title:
void showSum(int a, int b)

items: `void` means: the subprogram does not hand back a result.
`showSum` is the name.
The brackets hold the **parameters**: variables with a data type that get their values when the subprogram is called. You separate several of them with commas.

blocks.caption: The subprogram with the header line as its title. It calculates with a and b as if they were normal variables.

blocks.text: In the call box you write the values in the brackets, e.g. `showSum(3, 4)`. The first value goes into `a`, the second into `b`. Instead of numbers you can also use variables and calculations such as `showSum(x, x + 1)`.

blocks.caption: The main program calls showSum twice with different values. Open both diagrams and start the simulation here.

blocks.text: **Local variables:** The parameters and all variables created in the subprogram belong only to the subprogram. It gets **copies** of the values; more on that below under call by value. During the call, the simulation only shows the variables of the subprogram.
A subprogram can also hand back a result, the **return value**. Then the header line has the data type of the result instead of `void`:
int square(int x)
The statement `return result` hands back the value and ends the subprogram straight away. When you call it, you store the result in a variable: after `int q = square(5)`, `q` holds the value 25.

blocks.caption: The subprogram square calculates and hands back the result with return.
The main program stores the return value in q. Open both diagrams and try the simulation.

blocks.text: A subprogram with a return value has to end with `return`. If the return is missing, the simulation reports an error.

In the **code view**, the header line becomes a Java method (`public static int square(int x)`), a `def` in Python and a `function` in JavaScript. If the subprograms are open in other tabs, they appear in the code together with the main program.

exercise.title: Calculate the area

task.text: Build two diagrams. The subprogram `int area(int a, int b)` hands back the area of a rectangle, that is a times b. The main program asks for the length and the width, calls `area` and outputs **Area:** and the result. With 3 and 4, **Area: 12** appears.

hints: You build two diagrams: a subprogram that only calculates and hands back the result, and a main program for input and output.
Open a new tab with **+** and give it the title `int area(int a, int b)`. One statement is enough inside: `return a * b`. In the main program you type `int f = area(length, width)` into the call box.

steps.title: Copy or original: call by value and call by reference

blocks.text: What happens if a subprogram changes its parameter? That depends on **what** is passed.
**Call by value:** With `int`, `double`, `boolean`, `char` and `String`, the subprogram gets a **copy** of the value. If it changes its parameter, the caller's variable stays as it was.

**Call by reference:** With an **array**, the subprogram does not get a copy but a reference to the same array. If it changes a slot, the slot is changed for the caller too. The header line for this looks like this:
void clear(boolean[] seats)

blocks.caption: At the top, doubleIt gets a copy of number. At the bottom, row and seats point to the same array.

blocks.text: Try out both. Open the three diagrams and start the simulation in the main program:

blocks.caption: doubleIt only changes its copy x.
clear sets all seats to false, for example when a showing is cancelled.
number is still 5 after the call. The seats in row, on the other hand, are free after the call.

blocks.text: If you want to get a number back from a subprogram, use `return`, e.g. `number = doubleIt(number)` with the header line `int doubleIt(int x)`. An array, on the other hand, can be changed by the subprogram directly.

Strictly speaking, Java only knows call by value. But with an array, the whole array is not copied, only its **address** in memory. With the copied address, the subprogram finds the same array. It is as if I gave you a copy of my locker key: the key is copied, but the hay in the locker only exists once.

exercise.title: Bonus points

task.text: The main program calls `bonus(points)` and then outputs all the points. Build the subprogram `void bonus(int[] points)` that increases every score in the array by 1. Instead of 3, 5 and 8 you then see **4**, **6** and **9**.

hints: The main program is already finished. You only build the subprogram in a new tab.

Open a new tab with **+** and the title `void bonus(int[] points)`. Inside, a for loop runs over all slots and calculates `points[i] = points[i] + 1`. You do not need a return, because the array is changed directly.

blocks.text: Sometimes a loop should end **early**, in the middle of its body. That is what the **Break** is for. It leaves the loop it is in straight away. The program carries on with the first box after the loop. In Java, Python and JavaScript this is called `break`.
You recognise the Break by the point on its left edge. You can write a short comment into the box, e.g. `Leave the loop`. It appears in the code as a comment after `break`.
A Break almost always sits in a **branch**: the loop is only left if a condition is met.
A typical case is the **endless loop with a Break**. The loop itself has no condition. It runs until the Break is reached:

blocks.caption: The loop keeps asking for a number. With 0 it jumps out, otherwise it adds the number to the sum.

blocks.text: Without a Break, an endless loop would really never end.

The simulation runs the Break like `break`: it leaves the innermost loop and carries on after it. If a Break is outside every loop, the subprogram ends; in the main program, the whole program ends. `return` does the same.
Often you can do without a Break altogether: you write the stop condition straight into the loop. That is usually even clearer.

exercise.title: Sum until 0

task.text: Rebuild the program “Sum until 0” **without** a Break. It keeps asking for whole numbers until someone types 0. Then it outputs **Sum:** and the sum of all the numbers typed in.

hints: Without a Break, the condition of the loop itself has to check whether 0 was typed in.

Ask for the first number before the loop. The while loop runs with the condition `number != 0`. In the body you add the number to the sum and then ask for the next number. For the second input you only write `input: number "…"`, because `number` already exists.

blocks.text: In Java a subprogram is called a **method**. The square from above looks like this:
The main program calls the method by its name and passes the value in round brackets:

int q = square(number);
System.out.println("The square is " + q);

items: In the header, what the method returns (`int`) comes before the name. If it returns nothing, it says `void`.
The parameters go in the round brackets with their data type: `(int x)`. You separate several with commas.
In the Programming area you write every method in its own tab, just as every subprogram has its own structure chart.
In Java the exit is called `break`. With `while (true)` you build a loop that only ends through `break`.

exercise.title: Till with break

task.text: Write a till in Java. It keeps asking for a price in whole euros. At 0 it leaves the loop with `break`. Then it outputs how many items there were and what they cost altogether. For 3, 4 and then 0 you see **Items: 2** and **Total: 7**.

hints: You need two variables that start at 0 before the loop: one for the sum and one for the count.
Inside `while (true) { … }` you read the price. Right after that you check `if (price == 0) { break; }`. Only after that do you add the price to the sum and increase the count by 1.

items.text: I can split a big task into smaller problems.
I can insert a call and build a subprogram in a tab of its own.
I can pass values to a subprogram with parameters.
I can hand back a return value with return and store it when calling.
I can explain why a subprogram cannot change a number but can change an array.
I know what a Break does and why it sits in a branch.
I can end a loop with a Break or through its condition.
I recognise a method in Java and can leave a loop with `break`.

questions.question: What does a call box with the text `showResult()` mean?

options.text: The subprogram showResult() runs here, and then the program carries on.
The word showResult() is output here.

questions.question: Where does the program carry on after a Break?

options.text: At the start of the loop
At the first box after the loop
Right at the start of the program

questions.explanation: The Break leaves the loop it is in. In Java, Python and JavaScript it is called break.

questions.question: Why does a Break usually sit in a branch?

options.text: So that the loop is only left if a condition is met
Because otherwise a Break cannot be saved
Because a branch is a loop itself

questions.explanation: Without a branch, the loop would be left in the very first pass.

questions.question: Where does the simulation find the subprogram for a call `showResult()`?

options.text: It has to be in the same structure chart.
In an open tab with the title showResult()

questions.explanation: Build every subprogram in a tab of its own and give it the name from the call as its title.

questions.question: The subprogram has the header line `void showSum(int a, int b)`. Which call fits?
questions.explanation: Two parameters need two values. And `void` means nothing comes back that you could store.

questions.question: After `int q = square(5)`, q holds 25. What is at the end of the subprogram square?
questions.explanation: With return the subprogram hands the value back to the call. An output would only show it.

questions.question: `void doubleIt(int x)` calculates `x = x * 2`. The main program has `int number = 5` and then the call `doubleIt(number)`. What value does number have afterwards?
questions.explanation: Call by value: doubleIt only changed a copy of number.

questions.question: `void clear(boolean[] seats)` sets all slots to false. What is true for the array row in the main program after `clear(row)`?

options.text: It is unchanged, because the subprogram gets a copy.
All slots are false, because seats and row are the same array.

questions.explanation: Call by reference: an array is passed as a reference. The caller sees changes to the slots too.

questions.question: What is a subprogram called in Java?
questions.explanation: In Java a subprogram is a method, for example the `main` method. Depending on its kind, it is also called a procedure or a function.

questions.question: Many building blocks have a second name in textbooks. Match each term from VisuStruct to its other name.
questions.explanation: Both names mean the same thing. If you know one of them, you understand the other as well.

questions.question: What is written in the header of a Java method that returns nothing?
questions.explanation: void means “empty”: the method does something but returns no value.

lessons.title: Searching and sorting
lessons.summary: Use playing cards to understand how linear search, binary search and bubble sort work, and why some methods are much faster.

blocks.text: A pile of playing cards lies face down in a row in front of you. You are looking for the 9. What do you do? You turn over one card after another until you find the 9 or have turned over all the cards.

blocks.caption: The cards are mixed up. Every card you turn over is one comparison: is this the 9?

blocks.text: This is exactly how **linear search** works: it goes through the array from index 0 to the end and compares every slot with the value it is looking for. It always works, even if the values are mixed up.
In the array our cards are numbers. We leave out jack, queen and king.

blocks.caption: The loop runs until the card is found or there is no slot left. The variable comparisons counts how often a comparison was made. In the simulation, look for the 2, the 27 and the 4.

blocks.text: If the card is not there, `position` stays at **-1**. There is no index -1, so here -1 means “not found”.

exercise.title: Find a card

task.text: Create the array `int[] cards = {8, 4, 11, 4, 6}` and ask for a card. Output the position of the **first** matching card, e.g. `Position: 1` for the 4. If the card is not there, output `Not found`.

hints: Go through the array from front to back and compare every card with the one you are looking for.
Rebuild the example above. You do not need the variable comparisons here. The loop has to stop as soon as `position` is no longer -1, otherwise for the 4 you find the second one instead of the first.

blocks.text: Now the cards lie in front of you **sorted**, from small to large. You are looking for the 27. You no longer turn over the first card at the front, but the **middle** one:

items: If it is the one you are looking for, you are done.
If it is smaller, the card you are looking for can only be on the right. The whole left half drops out.
If it is larger, the right half drops out.

blocks.text: You do the same again with the rest. With every comparison the pile is halved.

blocks.caption: Three comparisons instead of fourteen: with every middle, half of the remaining cards drop out.

blocks.text: In the structure chart, two variables remember the range that is still being searched: `left` and `right`. The middle is `(left + right) / 2`. Because this is whole-number division, the result is always a whole index.

blocks.caption: The same array as for the linear search. In the simulation, look for the 27 again and compare the output Comparisons with the linear search.

blocks.text: Binary search **only works with sorted values**. With mixed-up cards, after looking at the middle you do not know which half to keep searching in.

I think of a number from 1 to 100. You may guess, and I only say “higher” or “lower”. With binary search you need at most **7** guesses. For a number up to a million it is at most 20, for a billion 30. Every doubling costs only one single extra guess. This is how databases search millions of entries in a fraction of a second. I search linearly, by the way: I eat the meadow from left to right.
How good a method is gets measured by the number of comparisons it needs **in the worst case**. For linear search, that is the case where the card is right at the back or missing.

blocks.caption: With 100 cards, linear search needs up to 100 comparisons, binary search at most 7.

blocks.text: Linear search grows at the same rate as the number of cards. With binary search, twice as many cards add only **one** comparison.

For binary search the values must be sorted. One of the simplest ways of sorting is **bubble sort**. You go through the row from left to right and always compare **two neighbours**. If the larger card is on the left, you swap the two.

blocks.caption: After one round, the largest card is on the far right.

blocks.text: After the first round the largest card is on the far right, like an air bubble rising to the top. That is where the name comes from. Then you repeat the round for the remaining cards. With 5 cards you need 4 rounds.

The structure chart has two for loops inside each other. The outer one counts the rounds, the inner one compares the neighbours `cards[i]` and `cards[i + 1]`. You already know how to swap: it needs a **temporary variable**.

blocks.caption: The inner loop gets shorter with every round, because the largest cards on the right are already in the right place. Go through it in the simulation with Step and watch the array under Variables.

blocks.text: Bubble sort is easy to understand, but slow. With n cards it needs up to n · (n − 1) / 2 comparisons: with 10 cards 45, with 100 cards already 4,950 and with 1,000 cards almost half a million. You may get to know faster methods such as quicksort later.

lessons.title: Structure chart and code
lessons.summary: All elements in Java at a glance, generate code, write Java in the Programming area, run it and find mistakes.

blocks.text: In lessons 4 to 19 you have already written every element in Java. Here you see everything at a glance and learn how VisuStruct turns a whole structure chart into a Java program.
A structure chart describes a process. For a computer to run it, you need a program in a programming language. VisuStruct writes this code for you.
Click Code in the tools (icon with angle brackets). On the right, the **Code generator** appears:

items: At the top you choose the language: **Java**, **Python** or **JavaScript**.
For Java you also choose under **Java output** between **Snippet** (only the statements) and **Class** (a complete Java file).
**Diagram text as comments** writes the text of every box as a comment above the code.
**Copy** puts the code on the clipboard, **Save Java…** saves a `.java` file.

blocks.text: The code changes straight away whenever you change something in the structure chart.
Later on, Nassi worked on the programming language Ada and was in charge of software at Apple. So if you invent structure charts, you do not end up in a goat shed, you end up at Apple.

blocks.caption: A small program with an input, a for loop and a branch. Open it and look at the Java code for it.

steps.title: This is the example in Java

blocks.text: For the diagram above, VisuStruct generates this code as a **Snippet**:
In Java every statement ends with a **semicolon** `;`. Whatever is inside a box goes in **curly brackets** `{ }` in Java. The indentation shows you what belongs together.

For input, `import java.util.Scanner;` and `Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);` are written once at the very top. Before every input VisuStruct outputs the question with `System.out.println(…)`.

If the false path of a branch is empty, VisuStruct still generates an `else` part that contains only the comment `// empty element`. If you switch off **Emit empty else branch in code**, the empty `else` part disappears.
You can paste a **Snippet** into the `main` method of an existing Java program. With **Class** you get a complete file that you can compile and run straight away:
The name of the class comes from the **title** of the diagram. The file must have exactly the same name, so here `TimesTable.java`. **Save Java…** takes care of that for you.

The generated code is a good start, but check it. If you first create a variable and later read it in again with an input, VisuStruct still writes `int pin = scanner.nextInt();`. Java then reports that `pin` already exists. Simply delete the `int` in that line.

Under the gear at the top right you can switch on **Code keywords**. Then the building blocks in the Elements area have the same names as the commands in Java: `if`, `switch`, `for`, `while`, `do`, `while(true)`, `break` and `call`. The rest of the interface stays in your language.
This helps you match the boxes to the Java commands. Your diagram itself stays unchanged.

So far you drew the structure chart first and then looked at the code. In the Programming area it also works the other way round. Click the slim **Programming** strip on the right. Next to the structure chart a column appears where you type Java yourself.

items: **Structure chart to code:** When you change something in the structure chart, the Java code changes right away.
**Code to structure chart:** When you type Java, VisuStruct builds the structure chart as you type. If something is still missing, for example a closing bracket `}`, a hint appears below the code.
**Suggestions:** While you type, VisuStruct suggests templates, for example for `if`, `for` or `while`. Press Enter to accept a template. Simply replace the grey placeholders with your own text.

**Indent:** If your code has got messy, click the **Indent** button at the top of the Programming area. Every level then sits four spaces deeper, as in Eclipse or IntelliJ. If you have selected lines, VisuStruct only indents those.

blocks.text: So you can try both ways. Drawing the structure chart first is good for planning a process. Writing code directly is faster when you already know what you want. The structure chart then helps you check your code.

At the top of the Programming area, ▶︎ Run starts your program and **■ Stop** ends it, for example in an endless loop. What your program outputs appears below in the console. If it asks for input, type it there and press Enter.
You can drag the border between code and console up or down with the mouse.

The Programming area understands the Java commands that also exist as boxes in the structure chart. It does not know your own classes and objects yet. Windows with Swing work anyway: turn on **Real Java (with Swing)** under the gear (lesson “Your first window”).

Professionals call a program where you write code, run it and look for mistakes an **IDE** (Integrated Development Environment). With the Programming area, VisuStruct is a small IDE with a built-in structure chart.
Sometimes a program runs but calculates something wrong. Then the **debugger** helps: it runs your program slowly while you watch.

items: **Breakpoint:** Click a line number on the left. A red dot appears. ▶︎ Run pauses before this line. Click again to remove the dot.
**Yellow line:** This line runs next. The matching box is selected in the structure chart.
**Variables:** Below the code you see the current value of every variable. Whatever changed since the last pause lights up yellow for a moment.
**Step:** The Step button next to ▶︎ runs exactly one line and pauses again. Without a breakpoint it starts the program and pauses before the first line.
**Continue:** ▶︎ runs to the next breakpoint or to the end. **■ Stop** ends it.

blocks.text: Try it with this program. Set a breakpoint on line 3 and press ▶︎ several times. How do `i` and `summe` grow?

This is a desk check, except the computer takes the notes for you. Before each step, think about which value the variable should have next. When the table doesn't match your guess, you have found the place with the mistake.

lessons.title: Python and JavaScript
lessons.summary: Generate Python and JavaScript code from the structure chart and run JavaScript straight in the browser.

blocks.text: In the code view (Code in the tools) you choose the language at the top. The structure chart stays the same; only the way it is written changes. That way you can compare the languages easily.

blocks.caption: A number is made smaller by 3 again and again until it is no longer greater than 0.

blocks.text: For the diagram above, VisuStruct generates this Python code:

number = int(input("Start value?"))
while number > 0:
    print(number)
    number = number - 3
print("End")
What is different in Python compared with Java:

items: There are **no semicolons** and **no curly brackets**. Python recognises what belongs to a loop or a branch by the **indentation** alone. After `while`, `if` and `else` there is a colon.
Variables get **no data type**: `int number = 5` becomes `number = 5`.
Output is called `print(…)`, input `input(…)`. For a number, `int(…)` goes around it.
In Python, arrays are called **lists**: `int[] numbers = {2, 4, 6}` becomes `numbers = [2, 4, 6]`, and `numbers.length` becomes `len(numbers)`.
A simple for loop such as `int i = 0`, `i < 5`, `i++` becomes `for i in range(5):`.

steps.title: What to watch out for in Python

blocks.text: In some places Python is stricter than Java. That is why VisuStruct translates the Java way of writing things when it exports:

items: **Text and number with +:** `"Sum: " + sum` becomes `"Sum: " + str(sum)`. Without `str(…)`, Python stops with an error.
**There is no i++:** it becomes `i += 1`.
**&&, || and !** are called `and`, `or` and `not` in Python, and `true` and `false` become `True` and `False`.
**Whole-number division:** In Python, `7 / 2` always gives 3.5. If the structure chart divides two `int` values, VisuStruct writes `7 // 2`, which gives 3, just like in Java.
**For loops:** Counting loops become `for … in range(…)`, also with `i <= n`, counting backwards or steps such as `i = i + 2`. If a loop does not fit that pattern, it becomes a `while` loop.
**There is no do-while:** it becomes `while True:` with `if not (…): break` at the end.

blocks.text: If a diagram is marked as **pseudocode**, only a note appears above the code. Then the text is a sketch and not a runnable program.
The same diagram in JavaScript:
JavaScript looks similar to Java: curly brackets, semicolons, `while (…)` and `if (…)`. The differences:

items: Variables are created with `let`, without a data type. Constants with `const`.
Output is called `console.log(…)`, input `prompt(…)`. `parseInt(…)` turns the input into a whole number.
Arrays go in square brackets: `let numbers = [2, 4, 6];`.
`"use strict";` at the very top makes JavaScript complain about typos in variable names.
JavaScript has only one number type. If the structure chart divides two `int` values, VisuStruct writes `Math.trunc(a / b)`. Then the digits after the decimal point are dropped, just like in Java.

blocks.text: JavaScript is the language of browsers. That is why VisuStruct can **run the code straight away**:

Why are links in the browser blue, anyway? In 1985 Ben Shneiderman's team tested which colour is easy to see but does not get in the way when you read. Light blue won. Red stood out more, but people remembered the text less well afterwards. [More fun facts](https://visustruct.org/en/angeberwissen.html)

items: Choose **JavaScript** in the code view.
Click **Test in browser**.
Whatever `console.log` outputs appears under **Output**. If the program asks for a value with `prompt`, type it in and click **OK**.
**Stop** cancels the program.

lessons.title: When the program crashes: try and catch
lessons.summary: Use real Java to read error messages and catch crashes with try and catch.

blocks.text: This program should print three grades. Type it into the Programming area and click ▶︎ Run:
The first grade appears, then it stops. VisuStruct reports “Invalid expression: grades[3]”, and “Done!” never shows up. The array only has the slots 0, 1 and 2; there is no slot 3.

Has this ever happened to you? One small mistake, and the whole program is gone. It happened to me so often that I cried in front of the screen. But there is a solution, and it is called **try** and **catch**.

In 1947 Grace Hopper's team found a moth in the Mark II computer at Harvard University that had caused a fault. They taped it into the logbook and wrote: “First actual case of bug being found”. Since then, program errors have been called **bugs**.
The Programming area normally calculates with the same simulation as the structure chart. It simply stops when there is an error. To see what real Java does, switch on real Java:

items: Click the gear at the top right and choose Java as the **Programming language**.
In the Java section, tick **Real Java (with Swing)**.

blocks.text: The first time you run a program, VisuStruct downloads about 40 MB once. After that your code is compiled and run just like in a real Java development environment.
With real Java, input from the console (`Scanner`) does not work yet. That is why our examples work without input.
Now write the program as a whole class, so that the line numbers match, and run it:
The console now shows:

First grade: 2
java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: 3
	at Grades.main(Grades.java:5)
A message like this looks scary at first. But it tells you exactly what is going on:

head: Part
Meaning
rows: The kind of error: the index is outside the array.
The line where it happened: line 5.

blocks.text: Java calls an error like this, at run time, an **exception**. We say: Java *throws* an exception. If nobody catches it, the program stops. That is why “Done!” does not appear.
Always read error messages from the top: first the name of the exception, then the line number. In the Programming area the line numbers are on the left next to the code.
With **try** and **catch** you catch the exception. Change the line with `grades[3]` like this:

items: `try` means “give it a go”. Java runs the block in curly brackets as usual.
If a line in it throws an exception, Java jumps straight into the `catch` block. The rest of the `try` block is skipped.
The brackets after `catch` say which exception is caught, plus a name for it, usually `e`.
After that the program carries on as normal. Now “Done!” appears too.

blocks.text: If everything in the `try` block goes well, the `catch` block is simply skipped.
try and catch are like the net under the trapeze at the circus: as long as everything works, you don't notice it. If someone falls, the net catches them and the show goes on.
The structure chart has no box for try and catch. So VisuStruct shows the whole block as one statement. You can only run it with real Java.
Often a number is text at first, for example later in a text field in a window. `Integer.parseInt` turns text into a whole number:

Java cannot convert “twelve” and throws a `NumberFormatException`. The program prints “That is not a number: twelve”. Change the first line to `String input = "12";` and run it again: now “Double: 24” appears.
This is not in the curriculum, but it is useful to know.
Every exception is an object of its own class, for example `ArithmeticException` for dividing by 0. `e.getMessage()` gives you its message, such as `/ by zero`.

A `try` may be followed by several `catch` blocks, one for each kind of error. `catch (Exception e)` catches all exceptions, but then tells you less about what happened. And a `finally { … }` block at the end always runs, whether there was an error or not.

lessons.title: Reading and saving text
lessons.summary: Read a text file line by line with Scanner and save a file with PrintWriter.

blocks.text: Everything stored in variables is gone as soon as the program ends. If a program should remember something, for example a game score, a list or grades, it saves the data in a **file**. The next time it starts, it reads the file again.
Zora is free, and Ludwig is planning a party. His shopping list is ready in the file `shopping.txt`:
A file ending in `.txt` contains only text, line by line. You can open it with any editor, for example Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on a Mac.
You already know the `Scanner`: `new Scanner(System.in)` reads from the keyboard. If you give it a file instead of `System.in`, it reads from the file:

head: Method
Meaning
rows: returns the next line and moves on by one line
closes the file when you are done

blocks.text: The loop runs as long as there is another line. In each pass, `nextLine()` fetches the next line. `File` belongs to the package `java.io`, so you need `import java.io.*;`.

blocks.caption: This is what reading looks like in a structure chart. Try it in the simulation.

blocks.text: Imagine the Scanner as a finger pointing at a line. `nextLine()` reads the line under the finger and moves the finger down one line. Once the finger is below the last line, `hasNextLine()` returns `false`.

steps.title: What if the file is missing?

blocks.text: If the file does not exist, Java cannot read it and throws a `FileNotFoundException`. Java insists that your program is prepared for this. Either you catch it with try and catch, as in lesson 22:
Or you write `throws Exception` after `main`. It means: "This method may throw an exception, I won't deal with it." Then the program stops if the file is missing.
public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
VisuStruct adds `throws Exception` after `main` automatically as soon as your program works with files. In the simulation, VisuStruct reports a missing file with "There is no file called …".

lessons.title: Line by line with BufferedReader
lessons.summary: Read with BufferedReader and readLine until null comes, and read a whole file at once with Files.

blocks.text: The morning after the party, Ludwig's cake has disappeared. Luckily the castle keeps a logbook. Every line starts with the day and the time:

blocks.name: logbook.txt
blocks.content:
Mo 08:15 Ludwig feeds the goats
Mo 12:30 Zora reads in the tower
Mo 18:00 Fox sneaks past the gate
Tu 09:00 Ludwig bakes a cake
Tu 14:45 Hare brings carrots
Tu 16:20 Fox asks for the recipe
Tu 23:55 The cake is gone
We 07:00 Zora finds crumbs at Fox's den

blocks.text: You could already read it with the Scanner from lesson 23. For files, though, professionals often use the **BufferedReader**.

items: `new FileReader("logbook.txt")` opens the file, and `new BufferedReader(…)` puts a buffer around it. It fetches the file in large chunks and is therefore faster for long files.
`readLine()` returns the next line. When there are no more lines, it returns **null**.
That is why the loop runs as long as `line != null`. At the end of each pass it reads the next line.

blocks.caption: First read a line, then check, then read the next one at the end of the pass.

blocks.text: **null** means "nothing at all". It is not the empty text `""`, but no text. A variable holding `null` has no methods: `line.length()` then stops with a `NullPointerException`. So always check `line != null` first.

The loop looks different from the Scanner one: the first line is read **before** the loop, every further one **at the end** of the pass. If you forget the read at the end, the program reads the same line again and again and never stops.

blocks.text: So that `close()` isn't forgotten even after an exception, there is a short form of try: whatever is created in the round brackets after `try` is closed by Java on its own at the end.
This is called **try-with-resources**. `IOException` catches all errors while reading and writing, including a missing file.
Like try and catch, try-with-resources only runs with real Java (lesson 22). In the simulation, you write `close()` yourself.
Since Java 11 it is even shorter. `Files.readString` reads the whole file at once, as you know from lesson 17. With `split("\n")` you split the text into an array of lines:
Now all lines are in the array. You can look at them in any order, for example backwards or only every second one.

steps.title: A table in a text file

blocks.text: Mrs Goat, the teacher at the castle school, has saved her class's grades as a table. As in Germany, 1 is the best grade and 6 the worst:
In the file, the table looks like this:

This is a **CSV file**. CSV stands for "Comma-Separated Values". Each line is a row of the table, and the columns are separated by a separator character. In English-speaking countries this is usually a comma, in Germany and many other countries a **semicolon** `;`, because the comma is already used in numbers like `2,5`. We use the semicolon.

items: The first line is the **header**. It says what is in the columns.
Every further line is a **record**, here one pupil.
Excel, LibreOffice and Numbers open CSV files directly as a table.

blocks.text: You know `split(";")` from lesson 17. It splits a text at every semicolon and returns an array:
Afterwards the grades are still **text**. You can only calculate with them once you have turned them into a number with `Integer.parseInt`:
int maths = Integer.parseInt(parts[1]);

blocks.caption: Split a CSV line and read the maths grade as a number.

blocks.text: For the whole file, you combine the BufferedReader from lesson 24 with `split`. The header contains no grades, so you read it before the loop and skip it:

Without the second `readLine()` before the loop, the header ends up in the loop. Then `Integer.parseInt("Maths")` tries to make a number out of the word, and Java stops with a `NumberFormatException`.

hints: Create `double sum = 0;` and `int count = 0;` before the loop. With `double`, nothing is cut off when dividing.
In the loop: `String[] parts = line.split(";");`, then `sum = sum + Integer.parseInt(parts[1]);` and `count++;`.

hints: Remember the best grade so far in `int bestGrade = 7;` and the name in `String bestName = "";`. Every real grade is better than 7.
If `grade < bestGrade`, remember the new grade and `parts[0]` as the name.

lessons.title: Data as JSON
lessons.summary: Understand JSON files, get values out with indexOf and substring, and write JSON yourself.

blocks.text: The castle zoo stores its animals in a file `zoo.json`:
This is **JSON**, the "JavaScript Object Notation". Almost every web app and every game sends and stores data like this. Unlike in a CSV file, each value has its **name** in front of it, the **key**.

head: Character
Meaning
Example
rows: an **object**: pairs of key and value
a pair, separated by a colon
a **list** of values, like an array
separates the pairs and the entries of a list
a text. Numbers and `true`/`false` have no quotation marks.

blocks.text: Objects and lists can be **nested**: the whole zoo object contains the list `animals`, and each animal is an object again. As with arrays, the list counts from 0: `animals[1].name` is `"Zora"`.

Professionals read JSON with a library, for example **Gson**. It is not part of Java and has to be added first. For our zoo file, the string methods from lesson 17 are enough, because each animal is on its own line.
In Java you write a quotation mark inside a text as `\"`. So the text `"\"name\": \""` is `"name": "`, exactly what comes before each name.

items: `indexOf("\"name\": \"")` finds the start of `"name": "`. That is 9 characters, so the name begins 9 characters further on.
`indexOf("\"", start)` searches for the next quotation mark **from** `start`. That is where the name ends.
`substring(start, end)` cuts out the name: `Zora`.

blocks.caption: Getting the name out of a JSON line.

steps.title: Exercise: All the names in the zoo

exercise.title: All the names in the zoo

task.text: Read `zoo.json` line by line. In every line that contains `"name"`, print only the name.

hints: Check with `line.contains("\"name\"")` whether there is a name in the line. Skip the other lines.
Inside the if: `int start = line.indexOf("\"name\": \"") + 9;`, then `int end = line.indexOf("\"", start);` and `System.out.println(line.substring(start, end));`.

blocks.text: To write, you put the text together with `+` and write it to the file with the PrintWriter from lesson 23. Texts in JSON need quotation marks, so `\"` in the Java text, numbers don't:
In a list there is a comma between the entries, but **none** after the last one. You check that with an if.
A single forgotten quotation mark or one comma too many, and no program can read the file any more. JSON is strict. That is why professionals also use a library for writing.

hints: Go through the arrays with `for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++)`. Build the entry with `"  {\"name\": \"" + names[i] + "\", \"points\": " + points[i] + "}"`.
If `i < names.length - 1`, add `","`. After the loop, write `"]"` and close the file.

Data can be nested, for example a list inside an object.
Java can't read JSON on its own. You need a library such as Gson.
JSON is the standard on the web. Almost every programming language knows it.
One character too many or too few makes the whole file unreadable.

lessons.title: Your first window
lessons.summary: Open your own window with Java and Swing, explained line by line.

blocks.text: So far your programs have written text to the console. Most programs you know, however, have **windows** with buttons and text fields. This is called a graphical user interface.
Java comes with a toolbox for this: **Swing**. In VisuStruct you switch it on like this:

items: Open the Programming area on the right.
Click the gear at the top right and choose Java as the **Programming language**.
Below that, in the Java section, tick **Real Java (with Swing)**.

blocks.text: The first time you click ▶︎ Run, VisuStruct downloads about 40 MB once, which takes a moment. After that your code runs as real Java, and your windows appear in the Programming area in the **Java windows** box above the console.
With “Real Java”, input from the console (`Scanner`) does not work yet. For programs with input, untick the box again.

Swing has been around since 1998. Before that, Java only had the older AWT with a class called `Frame`. So that nobody mixes up the new building blocks, almost all names in Swing start with **J**: `JFrame`, `JButton`, `JLabel`. The J tells you straight away that it is Swing.
This is the smallest program that opens a window. Type it into the Programming area and click ▶︎ Run:
An empty grey window with the title “My first window” appears. That's all, but it is your very own window!
You already know the frame with `public class` and `main` from the Java lesson. The first line and the four lines inside `main` are new. Let's look at them one by one.
Look at the structure chart next to the code: every line in `main` is a box, one below the other. So at the start, a window program is just a sequence.

head: Line
What it does
rows: Brings the Swing toolbox into the program. Without this line Java does not know `JFrame`.
Builds a new window. The text in brackets is the title at the top of the window frame. After that you talk to it through the variable `window`.
The window becomes 300 pixels wide and 200 pixels high.
When someone closes the window, the program ends too.
Only now does the window become visible.

blocks.text: The dot in `window.setSize(…)` means: “Window, do this!” Before the dot is who should do something, after it is what they should do.
Without `setDefaultCloseOperation`, Java only hides the window when it is closed. The program then keeps running invisibly.
`setVisible(true)` shows the window exactly as it is at that moment. So you set everything up first: title, size, and later buttons too. Only at the very end do you make the window visible.

Things you put into the window after `setVisible(true)` often do not appear. Java does not redraw the window on its own. Sometimes they only show up when you resize the window. Mistakes like that are hard to find.
Set up first, then show. Like in the theatre: the curtain only goes up once the stage is ready.
Try it: delete the line with `setVisible(true)` and run the program again. The program runs, but you do not see a window.
This is not in the curriculum, but it helps you understand Swing.

Java is really an **object-oriented** language. `JFrame` is a class, a blueprint for windows. With `new JFrame(…)` Java builds a real window from this blueprint, an **object**. With two `new` you could build two windows, both from the same blueprint.

`setSize` and `setVisible` are methods that every window object has. That is why you write `window.setSize(…)`: the object `window` runs its method. Your program itself is a class too, namely `MyWindow`.
Change the program so that

items: the title says “Hello” and your name,
the window is 400 pixels wide and 300 pixels high,
the program ends when you close the window.

blocks.text: Run it and check all three points.

Don't feel like typing so much? With “Real Java” you may type just the four lines from `main` into the Programming area. VisuStruct then wraps them in a class itself and adds the `import` lines. In a real Java development environment, though, you need the whole program.

lessons.title: A button in the window
lessons.summary: Put a button into the window and arrange it neatly with a layout.

blocks.text: An empty window is boring. Now a button goes in. In Swing a button is called **JButton**.
You need two new lines for it:

JButton button = new JButton("Click me");
window.add(button);

items: `new JButton("Click me")` builds a button. The text in brackets will be written on the button.
`window.add(button)` puts the button into the window. Without `add` the button exists, but it is not placed anywhere and you cannot see it.

blocks.text: Both lines go **before** `setVisible(true)`, because the window should be set up completely first and then shown:
Run the program. Surprise: the button is huge and fills the whole window!
The order is the same as with your first window: set up, build the button, put the button in and show everything at the very end. The empty lines in the code help you see these parts.
How a window arranges its parts is decided by its **layout**. Without further instructions, a `JFrame` puts everything in the middle and makes it as big as the whole window.
With a different layout the button gets its normal size. The **FlowLayout** places everything side by side like words in a line, only as big as needed:
`FlowLayout` belongs to the older AWT toolbox. That is why there is a second line at the top: `import java.awt.*;`.

With FlowLayout the building blocks flow like text: if a button no longer fits into the line, it moves to the next one. Make the window narrow and watch the buttons wrap. That is where the name comes from.
Click the button. It turns a little darker while you press it. So Swing shows that it was pressed. Apart from that, nothing happens.
That is not a mistake: you have not told the program **what** should happen on a click yet. You will learn that in the next lesson.
Build a window with the title “Button test”, 300 by 200 pixels, with a button “Click me” in normal size. It should be possible to press the button, even though nothing happens yet.
Extra: put a second button “Me too” next to it. In which order are the buttons? Swap the two `add` lines and try again.
Every button needs its own variable, for example `button` and `button2`, and its own `add`. FlowLayout places the buttons in the order of the `add` lines.

lessons.title: The button reacts
lessons.summary: Use an ActionListener to decide what happens on a click.

blocks.text: In the last lesson you could press the button, but nothing happened. In a window program it is the person who decides when something happens: they click, type or close a window. Each such action is called an **event**.

So your program has to wait for the click and notice it. For this you register a listener with the button, an **ActionListener**. On every click the button calls its listener, and the listener runs your code.
Until now your program ran from top to bottom, just like the structure chart. The code in the listener only runs later, whenever someone clicks. Nobody knows in advance how often that will be.
This is how you register the listener:
button.addActionListener(e -> button.setText("I was clicked"));
Read from the outside in:

items: `button.addActionListener( … )` registers a listener with the button.
`e` is the event. It contains, for example, when the click happened. You do not need it here, but the name has to be there.
Read `->` as “then do”.
`button.setText("I was clicked")` is what happens on a click: the button gets a new label.

blocks.text: The line comes after `new JButton(…)`, because the button has to exist already. And like everything else it comes before `setVisible(true)`.
Run it and click the button. Now it says “I was clicked”.
If the new text is longer than the old one, FlowLayout makes the button wider on its own.
If more than one thing should happen on a click, put curly brackets after the arrow. Inside, every statement has its semicolon, just like in a loop body:
`System.out.println` writes to the console as usual. Click several times: every click adds a new line “Click!”. That shows you that the code in the listener really runs on every click.
Watch the ending: first `}` closes the block, then `)` closes the bracket of `addActionListener`, then comes the semicolon. So `});`. If any of it is missing, a hint appears below the code.

steps.title: Expert knowledge: ActionListener is an interface

blocks.text: This is not in the curriculum. If you want to know what is behind the arrow, read on.

`ActionListener` is an **interface**, a kind of contract. It says: whoever wants to be an ActionListener must have a method `actionPerformed(ActionEvent e)`. On every click the button calls exactly this method.
You already know the line with the arrow from step 2:
button.addActionListener(e -> button.setText("I was clicked"));
Without the arrow you write the listener as a class without a name that fulfils the contract (an anonymous class):

For this you also need `import java.awt.event.*;` at the top. Both ways do exactly the same. The arrow `e -> …` is the short form (a lambda expression, since Java 8): `e` is the parameter of `actionPerformed`, and after the arrow comes its body. The short form works because the interface has only one method. So Java knows which method is meant.
Now you finish the task: build a window with a button “Click me” in normal size. After the click the button says “I was clicked”.
Extra: build two buttons “Red” and “Blue”. Clicking a button writes its name into the window title, for example “You chose Red”.
Every button gets its own listener with its own `addActionListener`. You change the title with `window.setTitle(…)`.

lessons.title: Doubling a number in a window
lessons.summary: Arrange a label, a text field and a button with a GridLayout and calculate with the text in the text field.

blocks.text: We build a small calculator with a window: at the top there is a label, below it a text field and a button **Calculate**. If you type 2 and click, the text field shows 4. Click again and it becomes 8, then 16 and so on.
For this you need two new building blocks:

items: **JLabel**: a label, simply text in the window.
**JTextField**: a text field you can type into.

blocks.text: As in the last lessons, tick **Real Java (with Swing)** in the gear.

steps.title: Three building blocks in the window

blocks.text: We put all three building blocks into the window, just like the button in lesson 29:
Run the program. Oops: all you can see is the giant button. Where are the label and the text field?

Remember the giant button? Without a layout of its own, a `JFrame` has only **one** place: the middle. Every `add` puts the new building block exactly there, as big as the whole window. So the three building blocks land on top of each other in the same place, and the window only shows the last one you put in: the button. You can't use the program like this.
The solution is a layout again. This time we use the **GridLayout**. It divides the window into cells of equal size, like a grid:
window.setLayout(new GridLayout(0, 1));
The two numbers are rows and columns. `0` rows means “as many as needed”, `1` column means: everything below each other. For `GridLayout` you also need `import java.awt.*;` at the top.

head: Layout
How it arranges things
rows: everything in the middle, on top of each other
side by side like words, with a line break when needed
below each other, every row the same height

blocks.text: Now all three are below each other. You can type into the text field and press the button. But the program doesn't calculate anything yet.

With `new GridLayout(2, 3)` you get 2 rows with 3 columns each, so 6 cells of the same size. That is how you build the keys of a calculator, for example. The building blocks fill the cells in the order of the `add` lines, row by row from left to right.

steps.title: Calculating with the text in the text field

blocks.text: On a click, the program should take the number from the text field, double it and write it back. Three methods do this:

items: `field.getText()` gives you the text in the text field, for example `"2"`.
`Integer.parseInt(…)` turns it into the number 2. You know this from lesson 22.
`field.setText(…)` writes a new text into the text field.

blocks.text: Together with the ActionListener from lesson 30 it looks like this:
`setText` needs a text. `"" + number * 2` appends the result to an empty text and so turns the number into a text.
Type “abc” into the text field and click Calculate. The window stays, but nothing happens, and the console shows a `NumberFormatException`. From lesson 22 you know what to do:
Instead of an error in the console, you now see a hint in the window.
The arrow already has an `e` for the event. That is why the exception in `catch` needs a different name, here `error`. Java doesn't allow two variables with the same name.

steps.title: Game: What is in the window afterwards?

blocks.text: Put the whole program together:

items: a window with the title “Double the number”, 250 pixels wide and 150 pixels high,
below each other a label, a text field and a button “Calculate”,
every click doubles the number in the text field: 2, 4, 8, 16, …
with “abc” a hint appears in the label instead of a crash.

blocks.text: Extra: a second button “Halve” divides the number by 2. What happens with 5?
The “Halve” button goes into the GridLayout as the fourth row and gets its own ActionListener. With `int`, Java cuts off the decimal places when dividing.

items.text: I can put a JLabel and a JTextField into the window.
I know why only the last building block shows without a layout.
I can arrange everything below each other with GridLayout(0, 1).
I can calculate with getText, Integer.parseInt and setText.
My program doesn't crash with “abc”.
