options.text: Because the label and the text field are missing
Because all building blocks lie on top of each other in the middle and the last one hides the others
Because the window is too small

questions.question: What does new GridLayout(0, 1) mean?

options.text: No row and one column, so the window is empty
As many rows as needed in one column, so everything below each other
One row, everything side by side

questions.question: What does field.getText() give you?

options.text: The text in the text field

questions.explanation: For a number you still need Integer.parseInt.

questions.question: Match each building block to its job.

lessons.title: Click counter with reset
lessons.summary: Two buttons change the same number: create a variable for the whole class.

blocks.text: A window counts clicks: the number is at the top, two buttons below it. **+1** counts up by one, **Reset** sets the number back to 0.
What's new this time: two buttons work with the **same** number. For that you need a variable that both listeners know.
Tick **Real Java (with Swing)** in the gear.
The obvious idea is to create the number in `main` as usual and count it up in the listener:
If you run this with real Java, the compiler reports an error:
local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final

The listener only runs later, on every click, long after `main` has finished. That is why it may read the variables from `main`, but not change them. Java insists: a variable from `main` that appears in the arrow must stay the same. For a number that changes on every click, we need a different place.

steps.title: A variable for the whole class

blocks.text: The solution: the variable does **not** go into `main`, but directly into the class, above `main`. Then it belongs to the whole class, and every listener may change it:

items: `static` means: the variable belongs to the class itself. Because `main` is `static` too, it is needed here.
A variable like this is called a **field** of the class. It lives as long as the program, not just as long as `main`.

blocks.text: `SwingConstants.CENTER` puts the text of the label in the middle. Click +1 a few times and then Reset.
With `number.setFont(new Font("SansSerif", Font.BOLD, 48));` the number becomes big and bold. `Font` comes from `java.awt`, which you have already imported.
Rebuild the click counter and extend it:

items: a button **−1** that counts down by one,
the number should never go below 0. If it is 0, −1 does nothing.

blocks.text: For “never below 0” the listener of −1 needs an `if`: only if `count > 0` does it count down.

items.text: I know why a listener may not change a variable from main.
I can create a static variable in the class.
Two of my buttons change the same number.
My counter has −1 and never goes below 0.

questions.question: Why may the listener not change the variable count from main?

options.text: Because numbers are not allowed in Swing
Because the listener runs later and Java doesn't let the arrow change variables from main

questions.question: Where does static int count = 0; go?

options.text: In main, at the very top

questions.question: What does SwingConstants.CENTER do in new JLabel("0", SwingConstants.CENTER)?

options.text: It puts the text in the middle of the label.
It puts the window in the middle of the screen.

lessons.title: A traffic light with colours
lessons.summary: Set background colours and switch a traffic light on with a state variable.

blocks.text: We build a traffic light: a large area lights up red. Each click on **Next** switches it on: red, green, yellow and red again.
New this time are **colours** and a **state**: the program has to remember which colour is currently showing.
Tick **Real Java (with Swing)** in the gear.
Colours live in the class `Color` from `java.awt`. Ready-made colours are, for example, `Color.RED`, `Color.GREEN`, `Color.YELLOW`, `Color.ORANGE` and `Color.WHITE`.
This is how you colour a label:

items: `setBackground(…)` sets the background colour.
A `JLabel` also needs `setOpaque(true)`. Without this line the background is transparent and the colour stays invisible.

blocks.text: `opaque` means “not see-through”. A label is normally transparent, like writing on a pane of glass. Only with `setOpaque(true)` does it get its own area that can be painted.

So that the traffic light knows what comes next, it remembers its state in a number: 0 means red, 1 means green, 2 means yellow. As with the click counter from lesson 32, the variable is in the class so that the listener may change it:
static int phase = 0;
On every click the phase moves on by one. After yellow (2) comes red (0) again:

This uses a new layout, the **BorderLayout**. It has five places: `NORTH` (top), `SOUTH` (bottom), `WEST` (left), `EAST` (right) and `CENTER` (middle). The middle gets all the space that is left. So the light becomes big, and the button stays narrow at the bottom.
BorderLayout is the layout a `JFrame` uses when you don't give it one. An `add` without a place lands in `CENTER`. That is why all the building blocks lay on top of each other in lesson 31.
Professionals switch on in one line: `phase = (phase + 1) % 3;`. The remainder operator `%` gives the remainder of a division. 3 % 3 is 0, so after 2 it starts at 0 again.
You now know three layouts. Each one arranges the building blocks differently:

head: Layout
How it arranges
Good for
rows: next to each other like words in a line, each block as big as needed
a few buttons in a row
a grid of cells of the same size, filled row by row
forms, keypads like on a calculator
five places: top, bottom, left, right and the middle, which gets the rest
something big in the middle, such as a picture or a display, with buttons at the edge

blocks.text: Without `setLayout` a window uses the BorderLayout. That is why everything then lands in the middle.

Ask yourself when planning: should all parts be the same size? Then GridLayout. Should one part be big and the rest narrow at the edge? Then BorderLayout. Should the parts simply keep their normal size? Then FlowLayout.

steps.title: Game: Where does the button go?

blocks.text: Rebuild the traffic light and make it more realistic. In the UK and Germany, red and amber light up together briefly after red. So add a fourth phase:

items: 0: red
1: red and amber (use `Color.ORANGE`)
2: green
3: amber (yellow)

blocks.text: Extra: in each phase, also write with `light.setText(…)` what the light means, for example “Stop” or “Go”.
With four phases, 0 comes after 3. So change the number in `if (phase > 2)`.

items.text: I can colour a label with setOpaque and setBackground.
I can remember a state with a static variable.
With BorderLayout I can put something big in the middle and something narrow at the bottom.
I know what FlowLayout, GridLayout and BorderLayout are good for.
My traffic light has four phases.

questions.question: Why does the colour stay invisible without setOpaque(true)?

options.text: Because a label is transparent otherwise
Because the window is too small

questions.question: Which place in the BorderLayout gets the space that is left?
phase is 2 and the listener runs phase++ and then if (phase > 2) { phase = 0; }. What is phase afterwards?
questions.explanation: After phase++ it is 3, which is greater than 2, so it becomes 0.

lessons.title: Grade calculator in a window
lessons.summary: Enter points, work out the grade with else if and catch wrong input.

blocks.text: A window turns points into a grade: you type the points of a test (0 to 100), click **Calculate grade**, and the grade appears at the bottom.
This time there is no new Swing building block. What's new is that you combine everything so far: text field, button, `else if` from lesson 20 and try/catch from lesson 22.
Tick **Real Java (with Swing)** in the gear.
We use this grading scale:
With `else if` you check from top to bottom. The first condition that is true wins:
With 85 points, `points >= 90` is false, but `points >= 80` is true. So grade B, and the remaining conditions are not checked at all. That is why the lower limit is enough each time.

You can try this part without a window in the Programming area. Put `int points = 85;` in front of it and `System.out.println("Grade: " + grade);` after it. The structure chart shows you the nested branches.
Two things can still go wrong:

items: Someone types “abc”. Then `Integer.parseInt` throws a `NumberFormatException`.
Someone types 150 or −5. That is a number, but not a valid score.

blocks.text: You catch the first case with try/catch, the second with an `if` before working out the grade:
`||` means “or” (lesson 9). The condition is true if the points are too small **or** too big.
Put the grade calculator together, with both checks from the last step. Test it with 90, 89, 0, 100, 101 and “ten”.
Extra: also write a word for the grade, for example “Grade: B (good)”. The words are excellent, good, satisfactory, poor and fail.
Always test the limits: 90 must be an A, 89 a B. Most mistakes hide at the limits, for example `>` instead of `>=`.

items.text: I can turn points into a grade with else if.
I can show the grade in the window.
My program reports “abc” and points outside 0 to 100.
I have tested the limits 90 and 89.

questions.question: Which grade does the scale give for 70 points?
questions.explanation: 70 is the lower limit for a C.

questions.question: Why is the lower limit enough in each condition?

options.text: Because else if has already sorted out the higher cases
Because Java doesn't know upper limits

questions.question: Which condition detects invalid points?
questions.explanation: A number can't be smaller than 0 and bigger than 100 at the same time, so you need or.

lessons.title: A calculator
lessons.summary: Two columns with GridLayout, four arithmetic buttons and catching division by 0.

blocks.text: We build a small calculator: two text fields for the numbers, four buttons **+**, **-**, **\*** and **/** and a line for the result.
New this time are **two columns** in the GridLayout and **several buttons** that all calculate with the same text fields.
Tick **Real Java (with Swing)** in the gear.
So far `GridLayout(0, 1)` put everything below each other. `GridLayout(0, 2)` gives you two columns. The building blocks fill the cells in the order of the `add` lines, always left first, then right:
You won't need the labels on the left later. So you can build them directly inside `add`, without a variable:

window.add(new JLabel("First number:"));
window.add(field1);

steps.title: The window with the first button

blocks.text: Type 3 and 4 and click +. The result shows 7.

Watch the brackets in `"" + (a + b)`. Without them Java works from left to right: `"" + a` gives the text “3”, and `"3" + b` appends the 4. You get “34” instead of 7. The bracket makes sure the calculation happens first.
The buttons -, \* and / work the same way. Only the operator in the last line changes:
/ has two special features:

items: With `int`, Java cuts off the decimal places when dividing. 7 / 2 gives 3.
If the second number is 0, Java throws an `ArithmeticException`, as in the task “Dividing safely” in lesson 22.

blocks.text: With `double` and `Double.parseDouble(…)` you get decimal places: 7 / 2 gives 3.5. In return, Java throws no exception when dividing decimal numbers by 0. The result is then `Infinity`.

steps.title: Expert knowledge: a method of your own

blocks.text: This is not in the curriculum, but it makes the code shorter.
Every listener reads the same two fields. You can move this repetition into a method of your own, a subprogram like in lesson 18. It goes in the class next to `main`:
`static int number(JTextField field) { return Integer.parseInt(field.getText()); }`
The listener then just says `result.setText("" + (number(field1) + number(field2)));`.

steps.title: Game: What does the calculator show?

blocks.text: Finish the calculator:

items: all four buttons calculate,
/ reports “Not by 0!” instead of crashing,
if a field contains “abc” or nothing, “Please enter two numbers” appears.

blocks.text: Extra: a fifth button **C** empties both fields and sets the result back to “?”.

For “abc” every listener needs a try/catch with `NumberFormatException`. A `try` may also be followed by two `catch` blocks, one for `NumberFormatException` and one for `ArithmeticException`. By the way, an empty field gives the text `""`, and that isn't a number either.

items.text: I can build two columns with GridLayout(0, 2).
I know why "" + (a + b) needs brackets.
All four arithmetic buttons work.
My calculator doesn't crash with 0 or “abc”.

questions.question: a is 3 and b is 4. What does "" + a + b give?
questions.explanation: Java works from left to right: first the text "3" is created, then the 4 is appended.

questions.question: What does 7 / 2 give with int?
In which order does GridLayout(0, 2) fill the cells?

options.text: Row by row, left first, then right
Column by column, starting top to bottom on the far left

lessons.title: Guess the number
lessons.summary: A game with a random number, a counter for the guesses and a button that switches itself off at the end.

blocks.text: Time for a game: the computer thinks of a number from 1 to 100. You guess, and the window tells you “too small” or “too big”. Once you have found it, it tells you how many guesses you needed.
New this time are **random numbers** and a button that **switches itself off** at the end.
Tick **Real Java (with Swing)** in the gear.
`Math.random()` gives a random decimal number from 0 to just under 1, for example 0.4173. Three steps turn it into a whole number from 1 to 100:
int secret = (int) (Math.random() * 100) + 1;
Without `+ 1` you would get 0 to 99.
Try it in the Programming area: `int secret = (int) (Math.random() * 100) + 1;` and `System.out.println(secret);`. Every run gives a different number.

Computers can't actually roll dice. `Math.random()` uses a formula to calculate a long sequence of numbers that only **look** random. They are called pseudo-random numbers. For games that is perfectly fine.
The game has to remember two things across all clicks: the secret number and the number of guesses. As with the click counter from lesson 32, both go in the class:

static int secret = (int) (Math.random() * 100) + 1;
static int guesses = 0;

items: `field.setText("")` empties the text field after each guess, so you can type the next one straight away.
`button.setEnabled(false)` switches the button off. It turns grey and can't be clicked any more. The game is over.

blocks.text: `setEnabled(true)` switches a button back on. That way you can, for example, only allow a button once something has been entered.

If you guess cleverly, you never need more than 7 guesses. Always guess the middle of the range that is left: first 50, then 25 or 75 and so on. Each guess halves the range: 100, 50, 25, 13, 7, 4, 2, 1. That is the **binary search** from lesson 19. Because 2 to the power of 7 = 128 is bigger than 100, 7 guesses are enough.
Rebuild the game and improve it:

items: An input like “abc” doesn't count as a guess and shows the hint “Please enter a number”.
A second button **New game** thinks of a new number, sets the guesses to 0, switches the Guess button back on and resets the hint.

blocks.text: Extra: after 7 wrong guesses the game is lost. The window then reveals the secret number.
For “doesn't count as a guess”, `guesses++` must come **after** `Integer.parseInt`, both in the `try` block. If `parseInt` throws an exception, the line with `guesses++` is skipped.

items.text: I can create a random whole number from 1 to 100 with Math.random.
I know which variables belong in the class.
I can switch a button off with setEnabled.
My game has a “New game” button.

questions.question: Which numbers does (int) (Math.random() * 100) + 1 give?
What does button.setEnabled(false) do?

options.text: It removes the button from the window.
The button turns grey and can't be clicked any more.
It changes the text on the button.

questions.question: With binary search, how many guesses do you need at most for 1 to 100?
questions.explanation: Each guess halves the range, and 2 to the power of 7 = 128 is bigger than 100.

lessons.title: Many buttons, one listener
lessons.summary: One listener for many buttons, and finding out with getActionCommand and getSource which button was clicked.

blocks.text: Since the business with the cake, Ludwig wants to lock his stable. He builds a **code lock**: nine digit keys, a zero, **C** to clear and **OK** to check. Only someone who types 1234 gets "Gate open!".
That's twelve buttons. Until now every button had its own listener, as with the calculator in lesson 35. Today you learn how **one** listener is enough for all buttons.
Tick **Real Java (with Swing)** in the gear.
With one listener per key it would look like this:
The lines only differ in the digit. If you want to change a small detail, you have to do it nine times and are bound to forget one line.
A listener can also be stored in a **variable**. Its data type is `ActionListener`, the contract from lesson 30. Then you sign up the same listener at several buttons:
`ActionListener` is in the package `java.awt.event`. So you need `import java.awt.event.*;` at the top.
Now the code exists only once. But how does the listener know which digit to add?
The `e` before the arrow is the **event**, an object of type `ActionEvent`. The button passes it along with every click, and it contains what happened:

head: Call
Returns
Example
rows: the caption of the clicked button, as text

items: `getActionCommand()` is handy when the caption already says what to do, as with the digits.
You compare `getSource()` with a button using `==`: `if (e.getSource() == ok)`. Here `==` is right, because it is about exactly this one object, not about a text.

blocks.text: You compare texts with `equals` and buttons with `==`. If you want to decide by the caption, you write `e.getActionCommand().equals("OK")`. That works too, but breaks as soon as someone changes the caption to "Open". `e.getSource() == ok` stays correct.
With a shared listener you can even build the digit keys in a loop. So that they line up neatly in a grid, they go onto a **JPanel**. A JPanel is an area in the window with its own layout:

items: `"" + i` turns the number `i` into the text for the caption.
Each pass creates a new button. All of them get the same listener `key`.
`window.add(keys, BorderLayout.CENTER)` puts the whole area with all the keys into the window.
`clear` and `ok` are created **before** the listener, because the listener compares with them.
The listener first checks the two special buttons. All the others are digits and add their caption.

blocks.text: The keypad on a phone has the 1 at the top left, the one on a calculator and a computer keyboard has the 7 at the top left. Why? When push-button phones came along, there were tests with people who had to dial with them. With the 1 at the top they were faster, and calculating machines had their layout long before that. Ludwig's lock does it like the phone.
Build the code lock and try it out.
Then make it better:

items: After three wrong attempts, **OK** switches itself off, like the button in Guess the number in lesson 36. Count the attempts in a `static int` variable in the class.
Extra: the display shows `*` instead of the digits. Remember the real input in a `static String input = "";` and only add a star to the display.

blocks.text: For the calculator from lesson 35, one listener is enough for +, -, \* and / too. Check inside it with `e.getActionCommand().equals("+")` which operator was clicked.

items.text: I can store a listener in a variable of type ActionListener and sign it up at several buttons.
I know what getActionCommand and getSource return.
I can put buttons onto a JPanel in a loop.
My code lock only opens with the right code.

questions.question: What does e.getActionCommand() return for a click on the button new JButton("7")?
How do you check whether the button ok was clicked?
questions.explanation: getSource returns the button itself, and you compare it with ==.

questions.question: Why is a listener stored in a variable?

options.text: So that you can sign it up at several buttons and write the code only once.

questions.question: Match.

pairs.right: the event e with the information about the click
an area with its own layout

lessons.title: Inner classes
lessons.summary: Write a listener as a named inner class, as an anonymous class and as a lambda, and know who can see what.

blocks.text: You already know the click counter from lesson 32. Today you write its listener in **three ways**, all of which do exactly the same:

items: as a **named inner class**, the way it was mostly done before Java 8,
as an **anonymous class**, which you know from the expert knowledge in lesson 30,
as a **lambda** with the arrow, as before.

blocks.text: In other people's code, in books and on the internet you will meet all three. After this lesson you will recognise them.
Tick **Real Java (with Swing)** in the gear.
A listener is anything that fulfils the contract `ActionListener`. It contains exactly one method:
public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e)
The button calls it with every click. The three ways of writing are three ways of providing this one method.
An **inner class** is a class inside another class. It has a name, here `Plus`, and fulfils the contract with `implements ActionListener`:

items: `new Plus()` creates an object of the class `Plus`. That is the listener the button gets.
Because the class has a name, you can use it for several buttons, here for `plus` and `again`.
The class is **outside** `main`. So it only sees what is in the class `Counter`: `count` and `number`. That's why `number` is a variable of the class this time and not of `main`.
You need `static class` because `main` is static. Without `static`, javac reports "non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context".

blocks.text: If you only need the listener in one place, you can write the class right where the object is needed. Then it gets no name:

items: `new ActionListener() { … }` means: "a new object that fulfils the contract ActionListener, like this: …".
At the end there is `});`: the curly bracket closes the class, the round one closes the call to `addActionListener`.
The anonymous class is **inside** `main`. So it also sees the variables of `main`, as long as they don't change any more.

blocks.text: The lambda is the short form of the anonymous class, since Java 8:

Everything Java knows anyway is left out: `new ActionListener()`, the name `actionPerformed`, `public void` and the type `ActionEvent`. What remains is the parameter `e`, the arrow and the body. This only works because the contract has exactly **one** method.
If a variable of `main` should change in the listener, like `count++`, it has to go into the class, whichever way you write the listener. That was the problem from lesson 32.

After compiling, look into the folder with the `.class` files. javac creates one file for every class: `Counter.class`, `Counter$Plus.class` for the inner class and `Counter$1.class` for the anonymous class. As it has no name, it gets a number. A lambda gets no file of its own, Java only builds it when the program starts.
Build the click counter with three buttons:

items: **+1** gets the named inner class `Plus`.
**-1** gets an anonymous class.
**Reset** gets a lambda.

blocks.text: Check that all three buttons count as expected. Then remove the `static` from the class `Plus` and read javac's error message.

items.text: I can write a listener as a named inner class.
I can write a listener as an anonymous class.
I know what is left out in a lambda.
I know which way of writing sees which variables.
My counter has three buttons written in three ways.

questions.question: Why does the short form with the arrow work for ActionListener?

options.text: Because the contract has exactly one method.

questions.question: Which way of writing can you use with new Plus() for several buttons without storing it in a variable?
Why is there static in front of class Plus?

options.text: So that the class is faster.
Because main is static and couldn't create an object of Plus otherwise.
Because every class has to be static.

lessons.title: Two tabs
lessons.summary: Build a window with two tabs, bring data from one tab to the other and save the list as a text file.

blocks.text: Ludwig's shopping list from lesson 23 gets a window. It has two **tabs**, like the tabs in a browser:

items: In the tab **Input** you type what you need and click **Add**.
The tab **List** shows everything you have entered. A button **Save** writes the list into a text file.

blocks.text: New are the tabs (`JTabbedPane`), a text area with several lines (`JTextArea`) and saving from inside a listener.
Tick **Real Java (with Swing)** in the gear.
Each tab shows its own area. The areas are JPanels, like the keypad of the code lock in lesson 37:

head: Call
Meaning
rows: a new tab with the caption "Input", it shows the JPanel `input`
switches to the second tab, counting starts at 0
changes the caption of the second tab

blocks.text: At the start, the tab that was added first is open.

steps.title: A text area with several lines

blocks.text: A `JTextField` has only one line. For the list you need a `JTextArea`:

items: `append` adds text at the end. The `"\n"` then starts a new line, as when splitting with `split("\n")` in lesson 24.
`setEditable(false)` stops people from typing into the list itself.
`getText()` returns the whole text with all lines.

steps.title: From one tab to the other

blocks.text: The button **Add** is on the tab Input, the text area on the tab List. Still, the listener can use both. All building blocks are variables in `main`, and the lambda sees all of them, no matter on which tab they are shown later:
A building block can only lie on **one** area. If you add the same button first to `input` and then to `list`, Swing takes it away from `input`. It only shows up on the tab List.

To save, you use the `PrintWriter` from lesson 23. Inside the listener there is a catch, though: the way out with `throws Exception` from lesson 23 doesn't exist here. The lambda is a method of its own, `actionPerformed`, and according to the contract it must not pass on a `FileNotFoundException`. That's why saving goes into try and catch:

items: The exception is called `ex` here, because the name `e` is already taken by the event.
After saving, the window jumps back to the tab Input with `setSelectedIndex(0)`, where the message is.
VisuStruct shows the saved file below the console as soon as you have clicked Save.

blocks.text: Type Hay, click Add, then Apples and Add again. Switch to the tab List and click Save.

steps.title: Game: Where does it end up?

blocks.text: Build the program and try it out.
Then make it better:

items: Empty inputs don't go onto the list. Check `field.getText().isEmpty()` first (lesson 17).
The tab List shows in its title how many things are on the list: "List (3)". Count along in a `static int` variable and use `setTitleAt`.
Extra: a third tab **Help** with a JLabel that explains how the program works.

I can add lines to a JTextArea with append.

lessons.title: Model View Controller
lessons.summary: Split the click counter into model, view and controller and understand who talks to whom.

blocks.text: Big programs with windows almost always share the same structure. It is called **Model View Controller**, **MVC** for short:

items: The **model** holds the data and knows its rules.
The **view** only shows the data.
The **controller** reacts to clicks and passes the word on.

blocks.text: You learn MVC with the click counter from lesson 32. It is split into three parts, step by step. In the end it shows the same count twice: as a number and as a bar.
Tick **Real Java (with Swing)** in the gear.
This is what the click counter looked like so far, everything sits in `main` and in one variable of the class:

That works. But imagine the count should also show up as a bar, later in a second window and in a file as well. Then every listener has to think of every display. Counting and showing are tied up in a knot, and with every display the knot gets bigger.
MVC unties the knot: every job gets its own class.
The model is the counter itself, without any Swing:

items: This time there is no `static` in front of `value` and the methods. That makes them belong to an **object**: `new Counter()` builds a counter with its own `value`, just as `new JButton("+1")` builds a button with its own caption.
`model.increase()` calls the method of this one counter, just like `button.setText(…)`.
Whoever wants to know the value asks with `getValue()`. It can only be changed through `increase()`.

blocks.text: As the model needs no window, you can try it out without a window at all:
The output is 2. Several classes may stand in one file. Only one of them is `public`, and that one contains `main`.
The view shows the value and does nothing else. It doesn't calculate, and it doesn't know where the number comes from:

items: The view is handed the value with `update(int value)` and writes it into its JLabel.
You build the window and the button in `main`, as always. `window.add(view.number)` puts the view's JLabel into the window.

blocks.text: The controller is the listener at the button. It connects model and view:

items: First it changes the model, then it fetches the new value and hands it to the view.

The problem from lesson 32 is gone: the variable `model` never changes, it always points to the same counter. Only the `value` inside it changes. That's why the lambda may use `model`, without any `static`.

blocks.text: With every click four messages run, always in the same order:

blocks.caption: The arrows light up one after the other. The model counts up at the second arrow, the display only at the fourth.

items: The button reports the click to the controller (`actionPerformed`).
The controller tells the model: `increase()`.
The controller asks the model for the new value: `getValue()`.
The controller hands the value to the view: `update(value)`.

blocks.text: The model talks to nobody. It waits until it is asked.
Remember: the model knows nothing about windows. In `Counter` there isn't a single `JLabel` and no `import javax.swing`. If you need Swing there, the code belongs in the view.
Now the count should also show up as a bar. For that a second view joins in. A `JProgressBar` is a bar that fills up, here from 0 to 10:
The controller gets one more line. The model stays exactly as it was:
That is exactly the pay-off of MVC: you can add or swap displays without touching the model.
Click +1 a few times and watch the number and the bar grow together.

MVC was invented in 1979 by the Norwegian Trygve Reenskaug, at the research centre Xerox PARC in California. Back then there were already computers with windows and a mouse there. In the same year Steve Jobs visited the lab and was so excited that Apple went on to build computers with windows and a mouse.

steps.title: Game: Where does the code belong?

blocks.text: Build the whole program and try it out.
Then make it better:

items: A button **−1** counts down. The model gets a method `decrease()` for it, the controller a second listener.
A button **Reset** sets the counter back to 0 with `reset()`.
The model itself takes care of the limits: never below 0 and never above 10, because then the bar is full.
Extra: a third view `ConsoleView` whose `update` prints "New value: 3" with `System.out.println`. A view doesn't have to be a window.

items.text: I can say what model, view and controller each do.
I can write a model without Swing and test it without a window.
I know what new Counter() builds and why there is no static.
I know the four messages after a click.
I can add a second view without changing the model.
My counter has −1, Reset and limits in the model.

questions.question: Where does the rule "The counter never goes above 10" belong?
questions.explanation: Rules about the data belong in the model. Then they hold no matter which button is pressed.

questions.question: What does the view do?

options.text: It shows the value it is given.

questions.question: Why may the lambda use model, even though model is a variable of main?

options.text: Because model always points to the same counter; only the value inside it changes.
Because lambdas may change any variable.

questions.question: What do you have to change in the model when a second view joins in?
Match.

blocks.text: Set two numbers, add them and output the result.

exercise.title: Add up

task.text: Set `number1` to the value 4 and `number2` to the value 3. Calculate the sum in a third variable and output only the sum.

hints: You need three variables: two for the numbers and one for the result.
You set a variable with a statement such as `int number1 = 4`. For the output you write the name of the variable without quotation marks.

blocks.text: A variable can change its value. Here a number is doubled.

exercise.title: Double a number

task.text: Set the variable `number` to the value 4. Double it in a second statement without creating a new variable. Then output **Doubled number: 8**, where the 8 comes from the variable.

hints: Doubling means: times 2. You store the result in the same variable again.
`number = number * 2` calculates with the old value and stores the result in `number` again. You join text and a variable with `+`.

blocks.text: In Germany, 19 % **VAT** (value added tax, a kind of sales tax) is added to almost everything you buy. The shop calculates with the net price (without tax) and adds the tax on top. That gives the gross price you pay at the till.

An example: you buy a folding phone that opens up into a tablet. The shop's price tag says 1000 euros net. On top of that come 19 %, so 190 euros. At the till you pay 1190 euros. The shop is not allowed to keep the 190 euros: it passes them on to the tax office.

blocks.caption: Net price plus VAT gives the gross price. The VAT goes to the tax office.

blocks.text: Baah, the shop bought the phone itself, of course: from the manufacturer for 800 euros plus 152 euros VAT. These 152 euros are called **input tax**, and the shop may subtract them from the 190 euros. So it only transfers 38 euros to the tax office. In the end only one person pays the whole tax: the customer at the till. That is you. I pay no tax at all, by the way. I just eat grass.

The tax rate never changes while you calculate. That is why you create it as a **constant**: a variable whose value stays the same once it is set. You write `const` in front of it, for example `const double VAT = 0.19`. Names of constants are written in capital letters so you recognise them straight away. In Java code this becomes `final double VAT = 0.19;`.
If the tax rate ever changes, you only have to change this one line.

exercise.title: Sales tax

task.text: Create the constant `VAT` with the value 0.19. Then ask for the net price. First output the tax and then the gross price, only the number each time. For a net price of 100 the outputs are **19** and **119**.

hints: The tax is 19 percent of the net price. The gross price is what you pay in the end.
The tax is `netPrice * VAT`. You get the gross price by adding the tax to the net price. Both values are decimal numbers, so `double`.

questions.question: Why do you create the tax rate as a constant?

options.text: Because its value should not change in the program
Because decimal numbers can only be stored as constants

questions.explanation: A constant keeps its value. If the tax rate ever changes, you only change the one line with `const`.

blocks.text: At the cinema, for a driving licence or for voting: it often matters whether someone is already 18.

exercise.title: Adult?

task.text: Ask for the age. If the person is 18 or older, output **adult**, otherwise **minor**.

hints: There are two possible outputs, so you need a branch.
Read in the age with `input: int age "How old are you?"`. The condition of the branch is `age >= 18`. Make sure that 18 already counts as adult.

blocks.text: A number is even if there is no remainder when you divide it by 2. You calculate the remainder with `%`: `8 % 2` is 0, `7 % 2` is 1.

exercise.title: Even or odd

task.text: Ask for a whole number. Output whether it is even or odd. For 4 the output is **4 is even**, for 7 **7 is odd**.

hints: A branch decides between even and odd. Even means: can be divided by 2 without a remainder.
The condition is `number % 2 == 0`. In the output you join the number and the text with `+`, e.g. `number + " is even"`.

blocks.text: In the school canteen you order by number. The program tells you which dish belongs to the number.

exercise.title: Menu

task.text: Ask for a number. For 1 output **Greek salad**, for 2 **Rice bowl** and for 3 **Falafel wrap**. For any other number output **Please choose a valid number**.

hints: A switch fits several fixed numbers. What happens with all the other numbers?
Read in the number with `input: int pick "Which dish?"`. The switch checks `pick`, and the cases are called `1`, `2` and `3`. All other numbers end up in the case `default`.

blocks.text: A small calculator: type in two numbers and an operator, and the result appears.

exercise.title: Calculator

task.text: Ask for two whole numbers and then for an operator as text: `+`, `-` or `*`. Output the result. For any other sign output **Unknown operator**.

hints: Read in all three values. A switch on the operator then decides what is calculated.

You read in the operator with `input: String operator "Operator"`. The switch checks `operator`, the cases are called `"+"`, `"-"` and `"*"`, and the last case is `default`. In every case, first calculate in a variable and then output it, otherwise `+` only joins the numbers together.

blocks.text: The Collatz sequence is a famous puzzle in mathematics. You start with a number and apply the same rule again and again:

items: If the number is **even**, you divide it by 2.
If it is **odd**, you multiply it by 3 and add 1.

blocks.text: So far, for every start number anyone has tried, the sequence ends at 1 at some point. Whether this is true for all numbers, nobody knows to this day.

exercise.title: Collatz sequence

task.text: Ask for a start number. Apply the rule until the number is 1, and output the new number after every step. Count the steps as you go and output **Steps:** and the count at the end. With the start number 6 the sequence is 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. That is 8 steps.

hints: You do not know how many steps there will be. That is why a while loop fits better than a for loop.
The while loop runs as long as `number != 1`. You check whether a number is even with `number % 2 == 0`. The output and `steps++` come after the branch, but still inside the loop.

blocks.text: This task could make you rich! The mathematician Paul Erdős offered 500 dollars for a proof. In 2021 the Japanese company Bakuage added quite a bit more: 120 million yen, about a million dollars at the time, for a proof or a counterexample. Nobody has collected the money yet. By the way, the puzzle was invented by the German mathematician Lothar Collatz in 1937. I am going to start calculating right now; that much money buys a lot of hay.
Computers calculate with only two digits: 0 and 1. This is how you convert a number into the **binary system**:

items: Divide the number by 2 and remember the remainder (0 or 1).
Carry on with the result without the remainder.
Repeat this until the number is 0.

blocks.text: The remainders read **from bottom to top** give the binary number. For 6 the remainders are 0, 1, 1, so the binary number is 110.

exercise.title: Binary number

task.text: Ask for a whole number greater than 0 and output it as a binary number. For 6 the output is **110**, for 13 **1101**.

hints: Keep dividing the number by 2 and remember every remainder. The remainders read backwards give the binary number.

Collect the digits in a text: `String binary = ""`. In the loop you calculate `int remainder = number % 2` and add the remainder at the **front**: `binary = remainder + binary`. After that, `number = number / 2`. Because number is a whole number, the remainder is dropped.

blocks.text: At a cash machine you have three tries for your PIN. If you type a wrong PIN three times, the card is blocked.

exercise.title: Check the PIN

task.text: The right PIN is 1234. Keep asking for the PIN until it is right or three tries have been used. Then output **PIN correct** or **Card blocked**.

hints: The loop ends in two cases: when the PIN is right or when three tries have been used. Count the tries.

The PIN is asked for at least once, so a do-while loop fits. Create `int pin = 0` and `int attempts = 0` before it. The loop repeats as long as `pin != 1234 && attempts < 3`. After the loop, a branch decides what is output.

blocks.text: With the Fibonacci numbers, every number is the sum of the two numbers before it. The sequence starts with 1 and 1:
You find these numbers surprisingly often in nature, for example in the way sunflower seeds are arranged.

Do you remember **swapping** from lesson 5? There you needed a helper variable, because `a = b` overwrites the old value of `a`. It is the same here: before `number2` gets the new number, its old value must be saved in `number1`. So watch the **order**: first `number1 = number2`, then `number2 = number3`. You will need this moving on and swapping again later, for example when sorting in lesson 19.

exercise.title: Fibonacci numbers

task.text: Ask how many Fibonacci numbers should be output. Then output exactly that many, each on its own line. You can assume that at least 2 is typed in.

hints: Every new number is the sum of the two before it. So you always have to remember the last two numbers.

Keep the last two numbers in `number1` and `number2` and output both before the loop. The loop starts at `int i = 2`. Inside it you calculate `int number3 = number1 + number2`, output it and then move on: `number1 = number2` and `number2 = number3`.

questions.question: Why must `number1 = number2` come before `number2 = number3` in the loop?

options.text: Because otherwise Java does not allow the assignments
Because otherwise the old value of number2 is overwritten before number1 gets it

questions.explanation: The other way round, number1 and number2 would have the same value afterwards. Just like swapping: first save, then overwrite.

blocks.text: How did you do lately? The average is the sum of all grades divided by how many there are.

exercise.title: Grade average

task.text: First ask how many grades will be typed in. Then read in exactly that many grades and output the average, only the number. For the grades 1 and 2 the average is **1.5**.

hints: You need the sum of all grades and how many there are. The average is the sum divided by the count.

The for loop runs from `int i = 0` while `i < count`. Inside it you read in a grade and add it to the sum. You store the average as a decimal number: `double average = sum * 1.0 / count`. The `* 1.0` makes sure that Java does not do whole-number division either.

blocks.text: Who is on board duty this week, cleaning the board? Five names go into an array, then a number is drawn.

exercise.title: Draw for board duty

task.text: Read five names into a String array. Then ask for a draw number from 1 to 5 and output **Board duty:** and the matching name. Draw number 1 belongs to the first name, 5 to the last one.

hints: First a loop reads in the five names. After that you do not need a loop any more, just one look into a slot.
You create the array with `String[] names = new String[5]`. Careful: the draw number starts at 1, the index at 0. So the name is in `names[pick - 1]`.

blocks.text: With `int pick = (int) (Math.random() * 5) + 1` you can also let chance draw the number. But for the automatic check we need a fixed input.
In the game Battleship the sea is a grid. The columns are called A to E, the rows 1 to 5. In the start diagram the sea is the 2D array `sea`: `true` means that part of a ship is on this square.

blocks.caption: Grey means `true`: there is a ship here. The small grey numbers are the indices in the array; they start at 0. In the game, on the other hand, the squares are called A to E and 1 to 5.

exercise.title: Battleship

task.text: Output all squares that have a ship on them, each square on its own line, e.g. **B1**. Go through the sea row by row with two nested loops. For the start diagram, **B1**, **C1**, **D1**, **E3**, **E4** and **A5** appear.

hints: Go through the sea with two nested loops, just like the cinema. Only output the squares that hold `true`.

The outer loop counts `row`, the inner one `column`, both from 0. If there is a ship on `sea[row][column]`, you output the letter from `columns[column]` and the row number: `output: columns[column] + (row + 1)`. You need the `+ 1` because the game starts counting at 1.

blocks.text: More than 2000 years ago, the Roman general Julius Caesar sent secret messages to his troops. His trick was simple: he replaced every letter with the letter **three places further on** in the alphabet. A becomes D, B becomes E and so on. The readable message is called the **plain text**, the encrypted one the **secret text**. The number of places you shift by is the **key**, often just called `k`.

blocks.caption: Encryption with the key 3: each letter at the top becomes the letter below it. At the end you start again from the beginning, so X, Y and Z become A, B and C.

blocks.text: This turns `HALLO` into `KDOOR`. Anyone who knows the key simply shifts three places back and can read the message again.
The cipher wheel

To avoid counting every time, people built a **cipher wheel**: two discs with the alphabet, a small one on top of a large one, fixed in the middle so it can turn. The outer ring shows the plain text, the inner ring the secret text. Turn the inner disc by three letters, and below every outer letter you find its secret letter. Wheels like this have existed since the 15th century. In the American Civil War (1861–1865), soldiers carried small brass wheels.

blocks.caption: A cipher wheel modelled on historical brass wheels. The blue window shows: with the key 3, D is below A.

blocks.text: Caesar himself didn’t even have a wheel! We know this from the Roman historian Suetonius: in his letters, Caesar shifted every letter by three places and simply counted it out in his head. The wheel was only invented by Leon Battista Alberti around 1467, about 1500 years later. By the way, I count in my head too. I don’t have fingers, only hooves.
Try it yourself. Turn the inner wheel, type a text and watch the secret text appear. **Decrypt** goes the other way.
LUDWIG

You can easily make a real wheel yourself: two circles of cardboard, one a bit smaller, each with 26 equal fields for the alphabet, and a paper fastener in the middle. Your secret agent tool is ready!

questions.question: What does the letter Y become with the key 3?
questions.explanation: After Y comes Z, then you start again with A and B. Three places further on is therefore B.

questions.question: A secret text was encrypted with the key 5. How do you decrypt it?

options.text: Shift it 5 places further on again

questions.explanation: Decrypting is the opposite of encrypting. By the way, 5 places back is the same as 21 places forward, because 5 + 21 = 26.

blocks.text: The program: there is more than one way

How do you teach the computer to shift a letter by `k` places? There is no *single* right solution. We look at two ways. Both go through the text character by character with a for loop, just like in the lesson on strings. The difference is how they shift a single letter.
In both ways the remainder operator `%` helps. It makes sure that after Z you continue with A: positions 0 to 25 stay as they are, 26 becomes 0, 27 becomes 1 and so on.
Way 1: the alphabet in an array

You put the alphabet into an array `char[] alphabet = {'A', 'B', …, 'Z'}`. For every letter of the word you search the array for its position `pos`, that is its index. The secret letter is then in the same array at position `(pos + k) % 26`.
An example with the key 3: X is at position 23. Then `(23 + 3) % 26 = 0`, and position 0 holds A.

exercise.title: Caesar with an array

task.text: The start diagram already contains the array `alphabet`. Ask for a word in capital letters and for the key `k`. Then output the encrypted word. For HALLO and 3 that is `KDOOR`.

hints: Create an empty text `String secret = ""`. Go through the word character by character with a for loop. In every pass you append one secret letter to `secret`.
To find the position of a letter you need a second, inner loop over the array: if `alphabet[j] == letter`, remember `pos = j`.
After the inner loop, append `alphabet[(pos + k) % 26]`: `secret = secret + alphabet[(pos + k) % 26]`. After the outer loop, output `secret`.

blocks.text: Way 2: calculating with the ASCII table

For the computer, every character is really a number. Which number belongs to which character is listed in the **ASCII table**. There A has the code 65, B the code 66 and so on up to Z with 90. In Java you turn a character into its code with `(int)` and a code back into a character with `(char)`:

int code = (int) 'A'
char letter = (char) 68
After that, `code` is 65 and `letter` is `'D'`. Changing a value from one data type into another like this is called a **type cast**.

Now you can calculate with the letter. So that the jump from Z back to A works, first subtract 65. Then A has position 0 and Z position 25, exactly as in way 1. Shift with `% 26` and add the 65 back at the end:

blocks.caption: At the top the capital letters with their ASCII codes. Below, the calculation for X with the key 3: the result is A.

exercise.title: Caesar with ASCII

task.text: Write a Java program that reads a word in capital letters and the key `k` and outputs the encrypted word. This time without an array: calculate with `(int)` and `(char)`.

hints: Go through the word with a for loop. You get the code of the character at position `i` with `int code = (int) word.charAt(i);`.
Calculate `code = (code - 65 + k) % 26 + 65;` and append the character: `secret = secret + (char) code;`. Before the loop write `String secret = "";`, after the loop `System.out.println(secret);`.

blocks.text: Which way is better?
**Way 1: array.** The idea is to search for the position in the array.

items: Advantage: easy to understand, and your own alphabets work too, e.g. with Ä, Ö and Ü.
Disadvantage: every letter has to be searched for.

blocks.text: **Way 2: ASCII.** The idea is to calculate with the character code.

items: Advantage: short and without searching, therefore faster.
Disadvantage: you need to know the ASCII codes.

blocks.text: Both programs give the same result. That is often how programming works: there are several correct solutions, and you choose the one that fits your task best.

exercise.title: Decrypt Caesar

task.text: Now turn the tables. Read a secret text in capital letters and the key `k` and output the plain text. For KDOOR and 3 that is `HALLO`. You decide which way to use.

hints: Decrypting means shifting `k` places back instead of forward. So `+ k` becomes `- k`.
Careful with A: `0 - 3` gives -3, and in Java `%` does not turn that into a positive number. So add another 26: `code = (code - 65 - k + 26) % 26 + 65;`

blocks.text: Unfortunately, Caesar is not secure. There are only 25 keys, and you can try them all in a few minutes. It is even quicker with a trick: in English, E is the most common letter. If H is the most common letter in the secret text, the key was probably 3. On the internet there is also ROT13, which is Caesar with the key 13. Applying ROT13 twice gives you the plain text again, because 13 + 13 = 26.
The age check from “Adult?” now becomes a subprogram of its own. The main program only calls it.

exercise.title: Age in a subprogram

task.text: Build two diagrams. The main program outputs **Welcome**, then calls `checkAge()` and finally outputs **Goodbye**. The subprogram `checkAge` is in a tab of its own: it asks for the age and outputs **adult** or **minor**.

hints: The main program has three boxes. The subprogram does the real work.

Open the exercise in the editor and build the main program there with the call `checkAge()`. Then open a new tab with **+** and give it the title `checkAge`. Build the input and the branch in it. Check finds the subprogram by the title of the tab.

blocks.text: At the rental machine you can book several vehicles one after another. The menu keeps coming back until you choose **0** to quit.

exercise.title: Rental menu

task.text: Keep asking for a choice: 1 = e-bike, 2 = e-scooter, 0 = quit. For 1 output **E-bike booked**, for 2 **E-scooter booked**, and for any other number **Invalid choice**. For 0 the program outputs **Bye** and leaves the loop with a Break.

hints: The menu runs again and again until someone chooses 0. An endless loop with a Break is good for that.

Use an endless loop. Inside it, first comes the input `input: int choice "1 = e-bike, 2 = e-scooter, 0 = quit"`, then a switch on `choice` with the cases `0`, `1`, `2` and `default`. The case `0` holds the output and, below it, the Break.
